# Netdryrun: full documentation

> Netdryrun is an open-source tool that tests network changes in a real virtual lab before they reach production. It boots the topology with containerlab, waits for convergence, checks BGP sessions, prefixes, routes and reachability, and returns a pass/fail verdict with evidence. It runs locally, in GitHub Actions, or as an MCP server for AI agents.

Install: `pip install netdryrun` · Source: https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun · Docs: https://netdryrun.com/



---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/

# Fail CI on routing mistakes before they reach production

To test a network change in CI, keep the changed configs and a containerlab topology in Git, describe the expected behavior in a `netdryrun.yml` file, and run `netdryrun run` (or the GitHub Action) on every pull request. Netdryrun™ deploys the lab, waits for BGP to converge, checks sessions, prefix counts, routes and pings, then destroys the lab. Any failed check exits non-zero and fails the job, with a JSON evidence file showing every command and its raw output.

!!! abstract "What Netdryrun is"
    Netdryrun is an open-source tool that tests network changes in a real virtual lab before they reach production. It boots the topology with containerlab, waits for convergence, checks BGP sessions, prefixes, routes and reachability, and returns a pass/fail verdict with evidence. It runs locally, in GitHub Actions, or as an MCP server for AI agents.

## A failing run

This is the bundled `frr-bgp-broken` example. Router r2 has a bad change: it sends r1 a default route.


```text
$ netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp-broken
Deploying lab ndr-frr-broken (3 nodes)...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is established (6.3s)
  [PASS] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (2.3s)
  ... (3 more passing checks trimmed)
  [FAIL] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- unexpectedly present via bgp (not selected) (0.1s)
FAILED: 5 passed, 1 failed (6 checks)
```

The leaked default route was *received but not selected*: r1 kept its own default, so traffic still flowed and the ping passed. A ping test or a config linter would have missed it. Netdryrun counts a route that is in the routing table but not selected as present, so the "must be absent" check fails.

The check that caught it:

```yaml
- type: route        # nothing should send r1 a default route
  node: r1
  prefix: 0.0.0.0/0
  protocol: bgp
  present: false
```

Checks like this one run only after the network has converged and must hold for a time window, so they cannot pass just because BGP has not come up yet. See [convergence semantics](reference/config.md#convergence-semantics).

## Run it in GitHub Actions

```yaml title=".github/workflows/network-dryrun.yml"
name: Network dry run
on: pull_request
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.0
        with:
          path: network/        # folder containing netdryrun.yml
```

The action installs containerlab, runs the checks, writes a summary to the job page, uploads the JSON and JUnit reports as an artifact, and fails the job if any check fails. Details: [GitHub Action](github-action.md).

## Run it locally

Fastest start on your own topology: `netdryrun record my-lab/topology.clab.yml --deploy` snapshots today's behavior into checks, then `netdryrun run my-lab` tests every change against it.


```bash
pip install netdryrun
netdryrun run path/to/folder    # the folder containing netdryrun.yml
```

Requirements: Linux or WSL2, Docker, containerlab, Python 3.10+. Walkthrough: [Getting started](getting-started.md).

!!! warning "What a lab cannot prove"
    A pass means the change behaved correctly in a lab built from container router images (FRR, Nokia SR Linux, SONiC, Arista cEOS). That is strong evidence for protocol logic and policy intent. It is not proof of:

    - vendor-specific behavior on the routers you run in production
    - behavior at production scale (full tables, many peers)
    - hardware and ASIC limits
    - timing and convergence at scale

    More on this in [Trust and security](trust.md#what-a-lab-cannot-prove).

## Status


Version 0.3.0, early. Works with FRR, Nokia SR Linux, SONiC and Arista EOS (bring your own cEOS image) on Linux and WSL2. Check types: `bgp_session`, `bgp_prefixes`, `route`, `bgp_route` and `ping` (IPv4/IPv6 unicast BGP sessions, prefix counts, routes, BGP best-path attributes and ping), plus link-down and node-isolation failure scenarios. On the [verdict corpus](corpus.md) (30 realistic BGP changes, expected verdicts committed before any run), Netdryrun judged 24/30 correctly, ping-only checks 20/30 and all-sessions-up checks 15/30. Issues and feedback: [github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/getting-started/

# Getting started

## Try it in your browser

No install: [open Netdryrun in GitHub Codespaces](https://codespaces.new/netdryrun/netdryrun?quickstart=1) and click **Create codespace**.

GitHub starts a Linux machine with Docker, containerlab 0.81.1 and Netdryrun installed from the repository, and pulls the FRR image the examples use. This takes a few minutes the first time. When the creation log shows `Ready`, run this in the terminal:

```bash
bash examples/agent-demo/demo.sh
```

The [agent demo](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/agent-demo) boots four FRR routers twice, which takes a little over a minute. The first change opens the filters to make a ticket work and is rejected by the leak guards; the second adds two prefix-list lines and passes all 14 checks. The run ends with `Demo OK`. The other FRR examples (`netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp`, `examples/frr-bgp-broken`) work the same way.

The codespace runs on the 2-core machine and uses your GitHub account's free Codespaces allowance (GitHub Free includes 120 core-hours and 15 GB of storage a month, so about 60 hours on this machine; Pro includes 180 core-hours). Stop or delete the codespace when you're done ([github.com/codespaces](https://github.com/codespaces)) so it doesn't use more. VM-based nodes (vrnetlab) don't work in Codespaces, which has no nested virtualization.

## Requirements

| Requirement | Notes |
|---|---|
| Linux or WSL2 | containerlab runs on Linux. On Windows, use WSL2. |
| Docker | The lab nodes are containers. |
| [containerlab](https://containerlab.dev/install/) | Netdryrun™ drives the `containerlab` CLI; it must be on `PATH`. |
| Python 3.10+ | |

containerlab needs root (or a user in the right groups) to create the lab. Run Netdryrun the same way you run containerlab on that machine.

!!! note "WSL2 and /mnt/c"
    If your topology lives under `/mnt/...` (a Windows drive), Netdryrun keeps containerlab's lab directory on the Linux filesystem (`~/.cache/netdryrun/labs`) unless you set `CLAB_LABDIR_BASE` yourself. SR Linux cannot save its config on a Windows drive.

## Install

```bash
pip install netdryrun
netdryrun --version
```

The MCP server for AI agents is included: run `netdryrun mcp`. See [AI agents](ai-agents.md).

## Run the examples

The repository ships these example labs (Arista needs your own cEOS image; SONiC pulls `docker-sonic-vs`).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun && cd netdryrun
netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp          # 3 FRR routers, should pass
netdryrun run examples/srl-frr          # SR Linux + FRR, should pass
netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp-broken   # a bad change, should fail
netdryrun run examples/sonic-frr        # SONiC + FRR, should pass
examples/agent-demo/demo.sh             # replay: a leaky change rejected, the fix accepted
```

Each run deploys the lab, runs the checks, prints one line per check and destroys the lab. Images are pulled on first use, so the first run takes longer.

### Expected results

The [examples page](examples.md) has every example, what it shows and how long it takes.


| Example | Topology | Checks | Expected | Exit code |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `examples/frr-bgp` | Triangle of three FRR routers (r1, r2, r3), eBGP | 2 sessions, prefix count 1 to 10, route present via BGP, ping, best-path AS path and next hop, default route absent, and a link-failure scenario (reroute via r3) | `PASSED: 11 passed, 0 failed` | `0` |
| `examples/srl-frr` | Nokia SR Linux (`srl1`) peering eBGP with FRR (`frr1`) | 2 sessions, a BGP route on each side, a ping in each direction, best-path attributes on `srl1` | `PASSED: 7 passed, 0 failed` | `0` |
| `examples/sonic-frr` | SONiC VS (`sonic1`, configured by `setup` commands) peering eBGP with FRR (`frr1`) | a session, a BGP route on each side, a ping, a prefix count, best-path attributes, a port-down scenario | `PASSED` | `0` |
| `examples/frr-bgp-broken` | Same triangle, but r2 adds `default-originate` toward r1 | The first 6 checks of `frr-bgp`, without the scenario | `FAILED: 5 passed, 1 failed`; the default route check fails | `1` |

The broken example is the one shown on the [home page](index.md#a-failing-run). r1 receives the leaked default route but does not select it, so the ping still works. The route check catches it because a received-but-not-selected route counts as present.

SR Linux takes longer to boot, so `examples/srl-frr` sets `timeout: 120`.

## Record a baseline of your own lab (fastest start)

Point `record` at any containerlab topology you already have:

```bash
netdryrun record my-lab/topology.clab.yml --deploy
```

It deploys the lab, waits for BGP to converge, and writes `my-lab/netdryrun.yml` with a check for every established BGP session, every prefix count and every BGP route (up to 50 per node). Then make your change and run:

```bash
netdryrun run my-lab
```

Anything that changed fails, with evidence. Before committing the baseline, remove what is allowed to change and add negative checks for what must never happen (for example `present: false` for a default route at a peer). See the [`record` reference](reference/cli.md#record) and the [tutorial](tutorial.md).

## Write checks for your own lab

Put a `netdryrun.yml` next to your containerlab topology:

```yaml title="netdryrun.yml"
lab: topology.clab.yml      # your containerlab topology
timeout: 90                 # seconds a positive check may wait for convergence

checks:
  - type: bgp_session
    node: r1
    neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  - type: route
    node: r1
    prefix: 192.168.3.0/24
    protocol: bgp
  - type: ping
    node: r1
    source: 192.168.1.1
    target: 192.168.3.1
```

Check the file without starting anything, then run it:

```bash
netdryrun validate .
netdryrun run .
```

To debug a failing run, keep the lab up with `--keep` (or `--keep-on-failure`), inspect the routers, and rerun the checks against the running lab with `netdryrun check .`. Destroy it afterwards with `containerlab destroy -t topology.clab.yml --cleanup`.

Next: the [tutorial](tutorial.md) walks through all of this on a real lab, step by step. Then see the [netdryrun.yml reference](reference/config.md), the [CLI reference](reference/cli.md) and [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/tutorial/

# Test a change on your own lab

This tutorial takes a containerlab lab you already have and turns it into a test for every change. You will:

1. record a baseline of how the lab behaves today,
2. review and prune it,
3. add checks for things that must never happen,
4. make a change and run the test,
5. read the evidence when it fails,
6. run the same test in GitHub Actions.

It takes about 15 minutes. Every command and output below is from a real run (Netdryrun™ 0.3.0, containerlab 0.81.1, FRR 10.4.1, on WSL2).

## Before you start

You need Netdryrun, Docker and containerlab. See [Getting started](getting-started.md#requirements).

## 1. Your lab

Any containerlab topology works. Here, the bundled `examples/frr-bgp` lab stands in for "your lab": three FRR routers in a triangle, each in its own AS, each announcing one LAN prefix over eBGP.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun
mkdir my-lab
cp -r netdryrun/examples/frr-bgp/configs netdryrun/examples/frr-bgp/topology.clab.yml my-lab/
sed -i 's/^name: ndr-frr-bgp/name: my-lab/' my-lab/topology.clab.yml
```

The folder now holds a topology and router configs, and no `netdryrun.yml`:

```text
my-lab/
  topology.clab.yml     # name: my-lab, nodes r1 r2 r3
  configs/
    daemons  r1.conf  r2.conf  r3.conf  vtysh.conf
```

The lab name (`name:` in the topology) must be unique on the machine. See [name collisions](troubleshooting.md#two-labs-with-the-same-name).

## 2. Record a baseline

`netdryrun record` deploys the lab, waits for BGP to converge, writes down what it sees, and destroys the lab.

```text
$ netdryrun record my-lab/topology.clab.yml --deploy
Deploying lab my-lab, then waiting 45s for the network to converge...
recording r1 (frr)
recording r2 (frr)
recording r3 (frr)
Recorded 18 checks to /home/dmin/ndr-docs/my-lab/netdryrun.yml. Review it, then: netdryrun run /home/dmin/ndr-docs/my-lab
```

This took 51 seconds. The file has one check for every established BGP session, every prefix count and every BGP route. The start of it:

```yaml title="my-lab/netdryrun.yml (recorded)"
# Recorded by netdryrun 0.3.0 record on 2026-10-27T04:38:28+00:00.
# This is a baseline of the network's behavior when it was recorded. Review it before committing:
# remove anything that is allowed to change, and add negative checks (route present: false,
# ping expect: failure) for things that must never happen. Docs: https://netdryrun.com/reference/config/
lab: topology.clab.yml
timeout: 120
checks:
- type: bgp_session
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
- type: bgp_prefixes
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  afi: ipv4-unicast
  exact: 2
- type: bgp_session
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.13.2
# ... 15 more: the same pattern for r2 and r3, plus one route check per learned LAN
```

## 3. Review and prune it

A recorded baseline says "nothing may change". That is rarely what you want. Decide what is allowed to change.

Here is what happens if you skip this step. The change in step 5 adds a LAN on r3. Run against the raw baseline, the `exact: 2` prefix counts fail, because r1 and r2 now get 3 prefixes:

```text
$ netdryrun run my-lab
Netdryrun 0.3.0: 18 checks from my-lab/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab my-lab (3 nodes)...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is established (10.3s)
  ...
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [FAIL] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 = 2 -- 3 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (0.2s)
  [FAIL] r1: prefixes from 10.0.13.2 = 2 -- 3 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (0.2s)
  [FAIL] r2: prefixes from 10.0.12.1 = 2 -- 3 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (0.2s)
  [FAIL] r2: prefixes from 10.0.23.2 = 2 -- 3 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (0.2s)
  [PASS] r3: prefixes from 10.0.13.1 = 2 -- 2 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.2s)
  [PASS] r3: prefixes from 10.0.23.1 = 2 -- 2 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.2s)
Destroying lab...
FAILED: 14 passed, 4 failed (18 checks)
```

The test did its job: something changed. But adding a LAN is allowed, so the baseline should allow it. Edit the file:

- **Keep** every `bgp_session` check. Sessions must stay up.
- **Turn exact prefix counts into ranges.** `min: 2` keeps today's routes; `max: 10` still catches a leak that floods r1. You can also record ranges from the start with `netdryrun record --min-prefixes`.
- **Keep the route checks you care about.** This tutorial keeps r1's and removes the r2 and r3 copies to keep the file short.

## 4. Add negative checks

`record` only writes down what exists. It cannot know what must never exist. Add those checks yourself. For this lab:

- nobody sends r1 a default route,
- the point-to-point link subnets (`10.0.x.x/30`) stay out of BGP,
- and a ping, so the test proves traffic gets through, not only that routes exist.

The reviewed file:

```yaml title="my-lab/netdryrun.yml (reviewed)"
# Baseline recorded with `netdryrun record`, then reviewed by hand.
lab: topology.clab.yml
timeout: 120
checks:
# Every BGP session stays up (recorded).
- type: bgp_session
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
- type: bgp_session
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.13.2
- type: bgp_session
  node: r2
  neighbor: 10.0.12.1
- type: bgp_session
  node: r2
  neighbor: 10.0.23.2
- type: bgp_session
  node: r3
  neighbor: 10.0.13.1
- type: bgp_session
  node: r3
  neighbor: 10.0.23.1
# Prefix counts may grow when a site adds a LAN, but not past 10 (recorded as exact: 2, edited).
- type: bgp_prefixes
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  min: 2
  max: 10
- type: bgp_prefixes
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.13.2
  min: 2
  max: 10
# Each LAN reaches the others (recorded routes; the r2 and r3 copies were removed to keep the file short).
- type: route
  node: r1
  prefix: 192.168.2.0/24
  protocol: bgp
- type: route
  node: r1
  prefix: 192.168.3.0/24
  protocol: bgp
# Added by hand: traffic gets through, not just routes.
- type: ping
  node: r1
  source: 192.168.1.1
  target: 192.168.3.1
# Added by hand: things that must never happen.
- type: route          # nobody sends r1 a default route
  node: r1
  prefix: 0.0.0.0/0
  protocol: bgp
  present: false
- type: route          # point-to-point link subnets stay out of BGP
  node: r1
  prefix: 10.0.23.0/30
  protocol: bgp
  present: false
```

Check it without starting a lab:

```text
$ netdryrun validate my-lab
OK: my-lab/netdryrun.yml (13 checks, lab /home/dmin/ndr-docs/my-lab/topology.clab.yml)
  - [bgp_session] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established
  - [bgp_session] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established
  - [bgp_session] r2: BGP session to 10.0.12.1 is established
  - [bgp_session] r2: BGP session to 10.0.23.2 is established
  - [bgp_session] r3: BGP session to 10.0.13.1 is established
  - [bgp_session] r3: BGP session to 10.0.23.1 is established
  - [bgp_prefixes] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 2 and <= 10
  - [bgp_prefixes] r1: prefixes from 10.0.13.2 >= 2 and <= 10
  - [route] r1: route 192.168.2.0/24 via bgp is present
  - [route] r1: route 192.168.3.0/24 via bgp is present
  - [ping] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success
  - [route] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent
  - [route] r1: route 10.0.23.0/30 via bgp is absent
```

To check BGP attributes too (communities, AS path, local preference, MED, next hop), add `bgp_route` checks; see the [reference](reference/config.md#check-types).

Negative checks are [post-convergence checks](reference/config.md#convergence-semantics): they run after the positive checks pass and a settle time, and must hold for 10 seconds.

## 5. Make a change and run it

The change: r3 gets a second LAN, 192.168.33.0/24. A first attempt announces it with `redistribute connected`:

```diff title="configs/r3.conf (first attempt)"
 interface lo
  ip address 192.168.3.1/24
+ ip address 192.168.33.1/24
 !
@@
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   network 192.168.3.0/24
+  redistribute connected
```

Run it, and ask for the JSON and Markdown reports:

```text
$ cd my-lab
$ netdryrun run . --json report.json --markdown report.md
Netdryrun 0.3.0: 13 checks from netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab my-lab (3 nodes)...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is established (14.0s)
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established -- state is established (14.0s)
  [PASS] r2: BGP session to 10.0.12.1 is established -- state is established (14.0s)
  [PASS] r2: BGP session to 10.0.23.2 is established -- state is established (14.0s)
  [PASS] r3: BGP session to 10.0.13.1 is established -- state is established (14.0s)
  [PASS] r3: BGP session to 10.0.23.1 is established -- state is established (14.0s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.2.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (14.0s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.3.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (14.0s)
  [PASS] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (need 2) (14.0s)
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [PASS] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 2 and <= 10 -- 6 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.2s)
  [PASS] r1: prefixes from 10.0.13.2 >= 2 and <= 10 -- 6 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.2s)
  [PASS] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- absent (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.2s)
  [FAIL] r1: route 10.0.23.0/30 via bgp is absent -- unexpectedly present via bgp (0.2s)
Destroying lab...
FAILED: 12 passed, 1 failed (13 checks)
  wrote json report: report.json
  wrote markdown report: report.md
```

The run took 37 seconds and exited with code `1`. Sessions are up, the ping works, and the prefix count is inside its range. Only the negative check caught the problem: `redistribute connected` also announces r3's link subnets.

## 6. Read the evidence

### Markdown report

`report.md` is the text the GitHub Action puts on the job page and in the PR comment. Failures come first, and each failure has the raw command output in a collapsed block:

````markdown title="report.md"
### ❌ Netdryrun failed

**12 passed, 1 failed** on lab `my-lab`

| | Check | Result | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| ❌ | r1: route 10.0.23.0/30 via bgp is absent | unexpectedly present via bgp | 0.2s |
| ✅ | r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established | state is established | 14.0s |
...
| ✅ | r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent | absent (held 10s, 5 samples) | 10.2s |

<details><summary>Evidence: r1: route 10.0.23.0/30 via bgp is absent</summary>

`r1$ vtysh -c show ip route 10.0.23.0/30 json`

```
{
  "10.0.23.0/30":[
    {
      "prefix":"10.0.23.0/30",
      "prefixLen":30,
      "protocol":"bgp",
      ...
```

</details>

<sub>netdryrun 0.3.0 · containerlab 0.81.1 · 2026-10-27T04:39:03+00:00 · full evidence in the JSON report</sub>
````

### JSON report

`report.json` has everything ([schema](reference/cli.md#json)). The top level says what ran and where:

```json
{"schema": "netdryrun.report/v1", "status": "failed", "lab": "my-lab", "error": null, "inconclusive_reason": null,
 "summary": {"passed": 12, "failed": 1, "total": 13}}
```

`environment` records the versions and images, so a result can be reproduced:

```json
"environment": {
  "netdryrun": "0.3.0",
  "containerlab": "0.81.1",
  "python": "3.10.12",
  "host": "Linux-6.18.54.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2-x86_64-with-glibc2.35",
  "nodes": {
    "r1": {"kind": "linux", "image": "quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1"},
    "r2": {"kind": "linux", "image": "quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1"},
    "r3": {"kind": "linux", "image": "quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1"}
  }
}
```

The failed check, with its history of samples:

```json
{
  "name": "r1: route 10.0.23.0/30 via bgp is absent",
  "type": "route",
  "params": {"node": "r1", "prefix": "10.0.23.0/30", "protocol": "bgp", "present": false},
  "passed": false,
  "detail": "unexpectedly present via bgp",
  "attempts": 1,
  "duration_s": 0.2,
  "history": [{"t": 0.2, "passed": false, "detail": "unexpectedly present via bgp"}]
}
```

Its `evidence` holds the command and the full output. The interesting part: the route is selected, installed, and points at r3 (`10.0.13.2`):

```json
{
  "10.0.23.0/30":[
    {
      "prefix":"10.0.23.0/30",
      "protocol":"bgp",
      "selected":true,
      "installed":true,
      "nexthops":[
        {"ip":"10.0.13.2", "interfaceName":"eth2", "active":true}
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

(Shortened; the report keeps every field.)

To look at the routers yourself, rerun with `--keep-on-failure` and run commands with `docker exec clab-my-lab-r1 vtysh -c "..."`, then destroy the lab with the command Netdryrun prints. [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#the-lab-never-converges-timeout) has an example.

## 7. Fix the change and run again

Announce only the new LAN, with a `network` statement:

```diff title="configs/r3.conf (fixed)"
 interface lo
  ip address 192.168.3.1/24
+ ip address 192.168.33.1/24
 !
@@
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   network 192.168.3.0/24
+  network 192.168.33.0/24
```

Add a check that the change did what it should, so the test also proves the new LAN arrives:

```yaml
# Added with the change: the new LAN reaches r1.
- type: route
  node: r1
  prefix: 192.168.33.0/24
  protocol: bgp
```

```text
$ netdryrun run . --json report.json --markdown report.md
Netdryrun 0.3.0: 14 checks from netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab my-lab (3 nodes)...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is established (13.9s)
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established -- state is established (13.9s)
  [PASS] r2: BGP session to 10.0.12.1 is established -- state is established (13.9s)
  [PASS] r2: BGP session to 10.0.23.2 is established -- state is established (13.9s)
  [PASS] r3: BGP session to 10.0.13.1 is established -- state is established (13.9s)
  [PASS] r3: BGP session to 10.0.23.1 is established -- state is established (13.9s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.2.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.9s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.3.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.9s)
  [PASS] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (need 2) (13.9s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.33.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.9s)
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [PASS] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 2 and <= 10 -- 3 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.2s)
  [PASS] r1: prefixes from 10.0.13.2 >= 2 and <= 10 -- 3 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.2s)
  [PASS] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- absent (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.2s)
  [PASS] r1: route 10.0.23.0/30 via bgp is absent -- absent (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.2s)
Destroying lab...
PASSED: 14 passed, 0 failed (14 checks)
  wrote json report: report.json
  wrote markdown report: report.md
```

38 seconds, exit code `0`. Commit the change and the updated `netdryrun.yml` together.

## 8. Run it on every pull request

Put the lab folder in your repository (here, `network/`) and add a workflow:

```yaml title=".github/workflows/network-dryrun.yml"
name: Network dry run
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "network/**"
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write   # only for pr-comment
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.0
        with:
          path: network/
          pr-comment: true
```

Every pull request that touches `network/` now deploys the lab on the runner, runs the checks, posts the Markdown report as a comment, uploads `report.json` as an artifact, and fails if any check fails. Make the job a required status check in your branch protection to block merges on a failure.

On GitHub-hosted runners, the `frr-bgp` example's CI job (install containerlab, pull the FRR image, run its checks including a link-failure scenario; measured on 0.2.0) takes 100 to 107 seconds. Before you open a PR with untrusted contributors, read the [Action security notes](github-action.md#security-notes).

- [netdryrun.yml reference](reference/config.md): every check type, including `ping` with `expect: failure` and failure scenarios (`link_down`).
- [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md): errors you may hit and how to fix them.
- [AI agents](ai-agents.md): let an agent run the same test before it proposes a change.
