# Examples

The repository's [`examples/`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples) folder has one lab per supported network OS, a deliberately broken change, and the AI agent demo. Each folder holds a containerlab topology, the router configs and a `netdryrun.yml`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun && cd netdryrun
netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp
```

## At a glance

Times are wall-clock for `netdryrun run` on WSL2 (20 cores, 16 GB) with images already pulled, measured on 2026-10-27 with containerlab 0.81.1 and Netdryrun™ 0.3.0 (`frr-bgp-broken` and `agent-demo`: 0.2.0; their checks did not change in 0.3.0). They include deploying and destroying the lab. The first run of each example also pulls its images.

| Example | Network OS | Shows | Expected | Exit | Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [frr-bgp](#frr-bgp) | FRR | Basic checks, best-path attributes, a leak guard, a link-failure scenario | `PASSED: 11 passed, 0 failed` | `0` | 84 s |
| [frr-bgp-broken](#frr-bgp-broken) | FRR | A leaked default route caught | `FAILED: 5 passed, 1 failed` | `1` | 45 s |
| [srl-frr](#srl-frr) | Nokia SR Linux + FRR | Mixed vendors | `PASSED: 7 passed, 0 failed` | `0` | 60 s |
| [sonic-frr](#sonic-frr) | SONiC VS + FRR | Configuring a NOS after boot, a port-down scenario | `PASSED: 8 passed, 0 failed` | `0` | 90 s |
| [arista-frr](#arista-frr) | Arista cEOS + FRR (your image) | A bring-your-own vendor image | `PASSED: 10 passed, 0 failed` | `0` | 92 s |
| [agent-demo](#agent-demo) `demo.sh` | FRR | An agent's leaky change rejected, the fix accepted | `Demo OK` | `0` | 65 s |

## frr-bgp

[`examples/frr-bgp`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/frr-bgp): three FRR routers (r1, r2, r3) in a triangle, each in its own AS, each announcing one LAN over eBGP.

**Shows:** the basic check types, a negative check and a failure scenario. r1 checks both BGP sessions, a prefix count between 1 and 10 (a leak guard), a route to r3's LAN, a ping to it, the AS path and next hop of the best path to r2's LAN (a `bgp_route` check), and that no default route arrives. The scenario takes the r1-r2 link down and checks that r2's LAN is still reachable through r3, that the best path now goes through r3 (AS path `65003 65002`), and that the session over the failed link is down.

**Expected:** `PASSED: 11 passed, 0 failed (11 checks)`, exit code `0`.

This is the lab the [tutorial](tutorial.md) uses as "your lab".

## frr-bgp-broken

[`examples/frr-bgp-broken`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/frr-bgp-broken): the same triangle, but r2's config (`r2-bad.conf`) adds `default-originate` toward r1.

**Shows:** a bad change being caught. Sessions are up and the ping still works, because r1 receives the leaked default route but does not select it. The negative route check fails anyway: a received-but-not-selected route counts as present.

**Expected:** `FAILED: 5 passed, 1 failed (6 checks)`, exit code `1`. The failing check:

```text
  [FAIL] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- unexpectedly present via bgp (not selected) (0.1s)
```

CI runs this example on every push and expects it to fail.

## srl-frr

[`examples/srl-frr`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/srl-frr): a Nokia SR Linux router (`srl1`) peering eBGP with FRR (`frr1`).

**Shows:** a mixed-vendor lab. Both sessions, a BGP route on each side, a ping in each direction, and the best path's AS path, local preference and next hop on `srl1`. SR Linux boots slower, so the file sets `timeout: 120`.

**Expected:** `PASSED: 7 passed, 0 failed (7 checks)`, exit code `0`. The SR Linux image is about 3.2 GB.

## sonic-frr

[`examples/sonic-frr`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/sonic-frr): SONiC VS (`sonic1`, the `docker-sonic-vs` image) peering eBGP with FRR (`frr1`).

**Shows:** a NOS that is configured after boot. SONiC VS has no startup config here; `setup` commands in `netdryrun.yml` wait for its services, set the interface addresses and configure BGP. Checks: the session, a route on each side, a ping, a prefix count, best-path attributes on `sonic1`, and a scenario that takes the SONiC port `Ethernet0` down and checks that the session drops and the route is withdrawn.

**Expected:** `PASSED: 8 passed, 0 failed (8 checks)`, exit code `0`. `setup` waits for SONiC's services before any check runs.

## arista-frr

[`examples/arista-frr`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/arista-frr): an Arista cEOS router (`ceos1`) peering eBGP with FRR (`frr1`).

**Shows:** a vendor image you bring yourself. cEOS-lab is free from arista.com with an account but can't be redistributed, so import it as `ceos:4.36.3M` first (the comment in `topology.clab.yml` shows how). Checks: both sessions, a prefix count, a route on each side, a ping, best-path attributes on `ceos1`, no default route at the Arista, and a scenario that takes the link down from the FRR side.

**Expected:** `PASSED: 10 passed, 0 failed (10 checks)`, exit code `0`. Without the image, the run stops with exit code `2`; see [the cEOS image is missing](troubleshooting.md#the-ceos-image-is-missing).

## agent-demo

[`examples/agent-demo`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/agent-demo): an edge router (`edge1`, AS 65000) with a customer, an upstream and a peer, a ticket ([`TICKET.md`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/examples/agent-demo/TICKET.md)) and the network team's 14 checks, including route-leak guards.

**Shows:** how an AI agent's change is judged. `demo.sh` replays two hand-written attempts: removing the prefix-list filters (passes the ticket checks, fails the leak guards) and adding the new block to two prefix lists (passes everything). See [AI agents](ai-agents.md#demo-a-ticket-a-tempting-change-a-verdict) and the [real agent run](ai-agents.md#a-real-agent-run).

**Expected:**

- `examples/agent-demo/demo.sh` exits `0` and ends with:

    ```text
    Demo OK: attempt 1 rejected by 5 leak guards with every other check passing; attempt 2 passed every check.
    ```

    Attempt 1 ends `FAILED: 9 passed, 5 failed (14 checks)`, attempt 2 `PASSED: 14 passed, 0 failed (14 checks)`. The two runs together took 65 seconds.

- `netdryrun run examples/agent-demo` shows the starting point, before anyone has worked the ticket: the guards pass and the 3 ticket checks fail, `FAILED: 11 passed, 3 failed (14 checks)`, exit code `1`. It took 119 seconds, because the failing ticket checks wait for their timeout.

## Use an example as a template

Copy a folder, change `name:` in `topology.clab.yml` (lab names must be unique on the machine), replace the configs with yours, and edit the checks. Or start from your own topology with `netdryrun record`, as in the [tutorial](tutorial.md).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/reference/config/

# netdryrun.yml reference

`netdryrun.yml` describes one lab and the behavior you expect from it. Commands accept either the file or the folder that contains it (`netdryrun run network/` reads `network/netdryrun.yml`).

```yaml title="netdryrun.yml"
lab: topology.clab.yml
timeout: 90
nodes:
  r1:
    driver: frr
checks:
  - type: bgp_session
    node: r1
    neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  - type: route
    node: r1
    prefix: 0.0.0.0/0
    protocol: bgp
    present: false
```

Validation is strict: unknown keys inside a check, missing required keys, bad IP addresses and bad values are errors (exit code `2`). Run `netdryrun validate` to check a file without starting a lab.

## Top-level keys

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lab` | yes | | Path to the containerlab topology file, relative to `netdryrun.yml`. The topology must have a `name`. |
| `timeout` | no | `120` | Seconds a positive check may wait for convergence. Each check can override it. |
| `checks` | yes | | List of checks. At least one is required. |
| `nodes.<node>.driver` | no | detected | Force the driver for a node: `frr`, `srlinux`, `eos` or `sonic`. See [drivers](#drivers). |
| `nodes.<node>.setup` | no | | Shell commands run inside the node after deploy, before any check. Each is retried every 5 s until it succeeds (the NOS may still be booting), within a shared 300 s budget. For NOSes that are configured after boot, such as SONiC. |

## Keys every check accepts

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | required | `bgp_session`, `bgp_prefixes`, `route`, `bgp_route` or `ping` |
| `node` | required | Node name from the topology (for example `r1`) |
| `name` | generated | Label used in reports. The default describes the check, for example `r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established`. |
| `timeout` | top-level `timeout` | Seconds this check may wait to pass. Positive number. |
| `hold` | `--hold` (10) | Seconds a [post-convergence check](#convergence-semantics) must hold. Positive number. |
| `vrf` | `default` | VRF (FRR) or network-instance (SR Linux) to look in |

IP addresses and prefixes are normalized, so `2001:db8:0::1` in YAML matches `2001:db8::1` on the device. Prefixes with host bits set are reduced to the network (`10.0.0.1/24` becomes `10.0.0.0/24`).

## Check types

### bgp_session

A BGP session reaches a state.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `neighbor` | yes | | Neighbor IP address as configured on `node` |
| `state` | no | `established` | One of `idle`, `connect`, `active`, `opensent`, `openconfirm`, `established`, or `down` (any state except established). Case-insensitive |

The check fails if the neighbor is not configured. A `state` other than `established` makes it a post-convergence check.

```yaml
- type: bgp_session
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
```

### bgp_prefixes

The number of prefixes accepted from a neighbor is within a range. Accepted means received minus rejected by import policy.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `neighbor` | yes | | Neighbor IP address |
| `min` | one of `min`, `max`, `exact` | | Lower bound, inclusive |
| `max` | one of `min`, `max`, `exact` | | Upper bound, inclusive |
| `exact` | one of `min`, `max`, `exact` | | Exact count |
| `afi` | no | `ipv4-unicast` | Address family: `ipv4-unicast`, `ipv6-unicast` or `evpn` |

Rules:

- At least one of `min`, `max` or `exact` is required.
- `exact` cannot be combined with `min` or `max`.
- `min` must not be greater than `max`.
- All three are non-negative integers.
- The session must be `established`. Counters reset to 0 when a session drops, so a count from a down session would satisfy `max` by accident; Netdryrun fails the check instead.
- If the session is established but the address family reports nothing, the count is 0.
- A check with `max` or `exact` is a post-convergence check. A check with only `min` is a positive check.

```yaml
- type: bgp_prefixes
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  min: 1
  max: 10          # guards against a route leak flooding r1
```

### route

A route is present in (or absent from) the routing table.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prefix` | yes | | IPv4 or IPv6 prefix |
| `present` | no | `true` | `false` means the route must be absent |
| `protocol` | no | any | Only count routes from this protocol. See [protocol names](#protocol-names). |
| `vrf` | no | `default` | VRF or network-instance |
| `active` | no | `true` | With `present: true`: `false` also accepts a route that is in the table but not selected (for example a BGP default losing to a local one) |

- **Present** means an *active* route matches: selected and installed on FRR, `active` on SR Linux.
- **Absent** means no matching route at all, active or not. A route that was received but not selected (for example a leaked default losing to a local one) still counts as present, so `present: false` fails. This is how the [failing example](../index.md#a-failing-run) is caught.
- `present: false` makes it a post-convergence check.

```yaml
- type: route
  node: r1
  prefix: 192.168.3.0/24
  protocol: bgp
```

### bgp_route

Attributes of the BGP **best path** for a prefix: communities, AS path, local preference, MED, next hop. Many real policy bugs live here: a route that is still present but lost its community, got the wrong local preference, or now goes the long way. `route` reads the routing table; `bgp_route` reads the BGP table.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prefix` | yes | | IPv4 or IPv6 prefix, matched exactly |
| `communities` | no | | The best path must carry **all** of these. Standard (`'65000:100'`), large (`'65000:1:2'`) or well-known names (`no-export`, `no-advertise`, `no-peer`, `blackhole`, `graceful-shutdown`, `accept-own`, `llgr-stale`, `no-llgr`, `no-export-subconfed`) |
| `without_communities` | no | | The best path must carry **none** of these. Same forms as `communities` |
| `as_path` | no | | Exact AS path, ASNs separated by spaces: `"65002 65003"`. `""` is the empty path of a locally originated route. AS sets are written `{65004,65005}` |
| `as_path_regex` | no | | Python regular expression searched in the AS path string, for example `"^65002 "` (learned from 65002) or `"(^| )65666( |$)"` (passes through 65666) |
| `local_pref` | no | | Exact local preference |
| `med` | no | | Exact MED. A path without MED counts as `0`, as best-path selection treats it by default |
| `next_hop` | no | | Exact next hop address |
| `present` | no | `true` | `false` means no path at all for the prefix in the BGP table, best or not |
| `vrf` | no | `default` | VRF or network-instance |

Rules:

- Without attribute keys, the check passes when a best path exists.
- **Quote communities.** YAML reads some unquoted values as numbers (`65000:10` is a base-60 number to YAML 1.1), so an unquoted community that YAML turns into a number is a config error.
- A community can't be in both `communities` and `without_communities`.
- `present: false` can't be combined with attribute keys. To forbid a community on the best path, use `without_communities`.
- The check fails if there is no path, or no best path (for example when the next hop is unreachable). The failure detail shows what the best path actually carries.
- **Local preference** is the effective value: a path without a LOCAL_PREF attribute (eBGP-learned or local) gets the device's default (FRR and SONiC: `bgp default local-preference`; SR Linux: the neighbor's `local-preference`; Arista EOS reports it directly). The exception is a locally originated path on Arista EOS, which reports no local preference; asserting `local_pref` on it fails with "not set".
- **Next hop** is the address the device reports. For an IPv6 path FRR may list only the link-local next hop.
- `present: false` and `without_communities` make it a post-convergence check: a "must not carry" check could pass on a transient best path before the real one arrives, so it must hold instead.

```yaml
- type: bgp_route         # customer routes are tagged and preferred
  node: r1
  prefix: 192.168.20.0/24
  communities: ["65000:100", no-export]
  local_pref: 200
  as_path: "65020"

- type: bgp_route         # the internal tag must never reach the peer
  node: peer1
  prefix: 192.168.20.0/24
  without_communities: ["65000:666"]
```

### ping

Reachability from a node.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `target` | yes | | Destination IP address |
| `source` | no | | Source IP address (passed as `ping -I`) |
| `expect` | no | `success` | `success` or `failure` |
| `count` | no | `3` | Packets to send. Non-negative integer. |
| `min_replies` | no | `count - 1`, at least 1 | Replies needed for `expect: success`. One lost packet is tolerated by default (first-packet ARP). |
| `vrf` | no | `default` | Runs in the VRF (`ip vrf exec` on FRR) or network-instance namespace (`srbase-<name>` on SR Linux) |

- `expect: failure` passes only with 0 replies, and is a post-convergence check.
- If ping did not run at all (bad source address, missing VRF), the check fails with an error. It never counts as a successful "failure".

```yaml
- type: ping
  node: r1
  source: 192.168.1.1
  target: 192.168.3.1
```

## Failure scenarios

`scenarios:` runs extra checks while links are down, then restores them. Use it to prove the network survives a failure, for example that traffic reroutes when an uplink dies.

```yaml
scenarios:
  - name: r1-r2 link fails
    link_down: {node: r1, interface: eth1}   # or a list of links
    checks:
      - {type: route, node: r1, prefix: 192.168.2.0/24, protocol: bgp}   # rerouted via r3
      - {type: ping, node: r1, source: 192.168.1.1, target: 192.168.2.1}
      - {type: bgp_session, node: r1, neighbor: 10.0.12.2, state: down}

  - node_isolated: r2          # all of r2's lab links down
    checks:
      - {type: route, node: r1, prefix: 192.168.2.0/24, present: false}
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | Label shown before each check (default: generated from the faults) |
| `link_down` | `{node, interface}` or a list of them. Interface names as seen inside the node (`eth1` on FRR, `e1-1` on SR Linux) |
| `node_isolated` | A node name (or list): every lab link of that node goes down |
| `checks` | Same check types as the top level, with the same convergence rules |

Scenarios run after the main checks, one at a time. Links are always restored afterwards, even if a check fails, and Netdryrun waits for the network to settle before the next scenario.

## Convergence semantics

Networks need time to converge, and some checks are trivially true before they do. Netdryrun splits checks into two groups.

**Positive checks** (session `established`, prefix count with only `min`, route present, ping expected to succeed):

- Polled every 3 seconds until they pass on **2 consecutive samples**, or until `timeout` expires.
- A single lucky sample is not enough. If the last sample passed but the streak was too short, the result says "not stable". If the check passed some samples but not consistently, the result says "flapping".

**Post-convergence checks** are the ones that would pass on a network that has not come up yet:

- routes that must be absent (`present: false` on `route` or `bgp_route`)
- best paths that must not carry a community (`without_communities`)
- pings that must fail (`expect: failure`)
- sessions expected in a state other than `established`
- prefix counts with an upper bound (`max` or `exact`), since 0 prefixes satisfies `max: 10` while BGP is still starting

They run after every positive check has finished plus a settle delay (`--settle`, default 10 seconds; at least 30 seconds if the file has no positive checks, because nothing else has shown that the network converged). Each one must then hold for the hold window (`--hold` or the check's `hold`, default 10 seconds), sampled every 3 seconds. A violation at any sample fails the check immediately.

Prefix counts with an upper bound first wait (up to `timeout`) for the count to enter the range, because counters ramp up, and then must hold.

Results are reported in the order the checks appear in the file.

## Drivers

A driver turns device state into a common shape. Netdryrun detects it from the topology:

- `kind: nokia_srlinux` or `kind: srl` uses `srlinux`
- `kind: arista_ceos` or `kind: ceos` uses `eos`
- `kind: sonic-vs`, or an image whose name contains `sonic`, uses `sonic`
- an image whose name contains `frr` uses `frr`
- anything else is an error unless you set `nodes.<node>.driver`

| Check | FRR | SR Linux | Arista EOS | SONiC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `bgp_session` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `bgp_prefixes` (accepted = received minus rejected by policy) | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `route` present / absent | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `bgp_route`: communities (standard, large, well-known), AS path, local preference, MED, next hop, absent | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `ping` success / failure | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Failure scenarios on the node's own links | yes | not yet (fail the FRR/Linux side instead) | yes | yes |

**Received-but-not-selected routes:** on SR Linux and Arista EOS, a BGP route that lost to a static or local route lives only in the BGP table, not the routing table. Both drivers read the BGP table too, so such a route still counts as present for `present: false`.

**SONiC:** `docker-sonic-vs` routes with FRR inside the container, so the `sonic` driver reads state through `vtysh` like the FRR driver. The image boots unconfigured; put interface IPs (`config interface ip add ...`) and BGP (`vtysh -c ...`) in `nodes.<node>.setup`. See `examples/sonic-frr`.

**Arista EOS:** cEOS-lab is free from arista.com (account required) and can't be redistributed. Download it yourself, then `docker import cEOS-lab-<version>.tar ceos:<version>`, and use `kind: arista_ceos` with that image.

| Driver | Source of state |
|---|---|
| FRR | `vtysh -c "show ... json"`; accepted prefixes from `acceptedPrefixCounter`; `bgp_route` from `show bgp <afi> unicast <prefix> json` |
| SR Linux | `sr_cli --output-format json "info from state ..."`; accepted = `received-routes` minus `rejected-routes`; `bgp_route` from the `bgp-rib` local RIB and its `attr-sets` |
| Arista EOS | `Cli -c "show ... \| json"`; `bgp_route` from `show ip bgp <prefix> vrf <vrf>` (the best path is the `active` one) |
| SONiC | the FRR commands, through `vtysh` inside the container |

If a driver can't read a `bgp_route` attribute, the run stops before deploying with "`<key>` is not supported on `<driver>`" (exit code `2`) instead of guessing. Today every driver reads every attribute.

Every command and its raw output is kept in the [JSON report](cli.md#json).

## Protocol names

`protocol` on a route check is compared in lower case with the protocol the device reports, after normalization:

| Use | FRR reports | SR Linux reports |
|---|---|---|
| `bgp` | `bgp` | `bgp` |
| `static` | `static` | `static` |
| `connected` | `connected` | `local` |
| `local` | `local` | `host` |
| `ospf` | `ospf` | `ospfv2` |
| `ospf6` | `ospf6` | `ospfv3` |
| `isis` | `isis` | `isis` |

Other protocol names are passed through in lower case as the device reports them. The failure detail lists the protocols that were seen, which helps when a name does not match.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/reference/cli/

# CLI and reports

```text
netdryrun run      [path] [options]   deploy the lab, run checks, destroy the lab
netdryrun check    [path] [options]   run checks against an already running lab
netdryrun validate [path]             validate netdryrun.yml without running anything
netdryrun --version
```

`path` is `netdryrun.yml` or the folder containing it. Default: the current folder.

## Commands

### run

Deploys the containerlab topology (`containerlab deploy --reconfigure`), runs every check, writes reports, and destroys the lab (`containerlab destroy --cleanup`). The lab is destroyed even when checks fail, unless you ask to keep it.

### check

Runs the checks against a lab that is already up, for example one left running with `--keep`. It does not deploy or destroy anything. It fails with an error if any of the lab's containers are not running.

### validate

Loads and validates `netdryrun.yml` and prints the parsed checks. It does not need Docker or containerlab to be running.

```text
$ netdryrun validate examples/frr-bgp
OK: examples/frr-bgp/netdryrun.yml (7 checks, lab .../examples/frr-bgp/topology.clab.yml)
  - [bgp_session] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established
  ...
```

### record

```bash
netdryrun record path/to/topology.clab.yml --deploy
```

Snapshots a known-good lab into a `netdryrun.yml` baseline: every established BGP session, every prefix count (exact, or minimums with `--min-prefixes`) and up to 50 BGP routes per node. Commit it, and every later change is tested against today's behavior. Review the file before committing: remove what is allowed to change, and add negative checks for what must never happen.

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out FILE` | Where to write (default: `netdryrun.yml` next to the topology) |
| `--deploy` | Deploy the lab first and destroy it afterwards (otherwise the lab must be running) |
| `--wait SECONDS` | With `--deploy`: time for BGP to converge before recording (default 45) |
| `--min-prefixes` | Record prefix counts as minimums instead of exact |
| `--no-routes` | Don't record individual routes |
| `--attributes` | Also record a `bgp_route` check per BGP route, pinning its best path's AS path, local preference and communities (not MED or next hop, which follow the topology) |
| `--force` | Overwrite an existing file |

## Options

`run` and `check`:

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--json FILE` | | Write the full evidence report as JSON |
| `--markdown FILE` | | Write a Markdown summary (for PR comments) |
| `--junit FILE` | | Write JUnit XML (for CI test reporting) |
| `--settle SECONDS` | `10` | Wait before post-convergence checks |
| `--hold SECONDS` | `10` | How long a post-convergence check must hold (a check's own `hold` key overrides it) |
| `--no-step-summary` | | Do not append the Markdown summary to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` |

`run` only:

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--keep` | Leave the lab running afterwards, for debugging |
| `--keep-on-failure` | Leave the lab running only if the run did not pass |

When a lab is kept, Netdryrun prints the command to destroy it. See [convergence semantics](config.md#convergence-semantics) for what `--settle` and `--hold` control.

## Exit codes

| Code | Status | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `0` | `passed` | Every check passed |
| `1` | `failed` | At least one check failed |
| `2` | `error` | Config error, or the lab could not be deployed or reached (containerlab or Docker missing, deploy failed, containers not running, unknown driver) |
| `3` | `inconclusive` | Checks failed, but the lab never reached a state where they mean anything: the result says nothing about the change. Rules below |

### When a run is inconclusive

A run is `inconclusive` instead of `failed` only when **all** of these hold. The rules are deliberately conservative: when in doubt, the run is `failed`.

1. At least one check failed, and there was no lab or config error (that is `error`).
2. No positive check passed on **any** sample, anywhere in the run, scenarios included. One passing sample anywhere shows a working network, so the failures are findings.
3. No post-convergence check failed with readable state. A leaked route, or a session that is up but must be down, proves a working control plane.
4. Every failed check is on a node that never gave usable state. That means every sample of every `bgp_session` and `bgp_prefixes` check on the node was *unready*: the state command failed or its output could not be read (a CLI that isn't up yet), or BGP had no neighbors at all on the node. A node with no session or prefix checks qualifies only if every sample of every check on it was unready.

A configured BGP session that is down (`idle`, `active`, `connect`, ...) is never unready. An ASN typo, a wrong neighbor address or a shutdown look exactly like a slow lab from the outside, so they stay `failed`. A routing table without the route, and a ping with no replies, are findings for the same reason. So a `timeout` that is merely too short for configured sessions to establish gives `failed`, not `inconclusive`; `inconclusive` is for a node whose CLI or BGP never came up at all.

Known limit: a change that deletes a node's entire BGP configuration looks like a NOS that never started BGP, so it is reported `inconclusive`. It is still never `passed`.

What to do: rerun, raise `timeout`, or check that the lab boots (`containerlab inspect`). Don't change the network change because of an inconclusive run.

The JSON report says why in `inconclusive_reason`, and each unready sample in `history` has `"unready": true`.

## GitHub Actions step summary

When the `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` environment variable is set (it is in GitHub Actions), the Markdown summary is appended to the job page automatically. Use `--no-step-summary` to turn this off.

## Report formats

### Console

One line per check as it finishes, then a summary line:

```text
  [FAIL] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- unexpectedly present via bgp (not selected) (0.1s)
FAILED: 5 passed, 1 failed (6 checks)
```

### JSON

`--json FILE` writes the full evidence. Schema identifier: `netdryrun.report/v1`.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `schema` | string | Always `netdryrun.report/v1` |
| `status` | string | `passed`, `failed`, `error` or `inconclusive` (new after 0.2.0; a reader should treat any status it does not know as not passed) |
| `lab` | string | containerlab lab name |
| `config` | string | Path of the `netdryrun.yml` that was run |
| `started`, `finished` | string | UTC timestamps (ISO 8601) |
| `error` | string or null | Lab or driver error, if the run could not complete |
| `inconclusive_reason` | string or null | Why the run is `inconclusive` ([rules](#when-a-run-is-inconclusive)); null otherwise |
| `environment` | object | `netdryrun`, `containerlab` and `python` versions, `host` platform, and `nodes` (each with `kind` and `image`) |
| `summary` | object | `passed`, `failed`, `total` |
| `checks` | array | One object per check, in file order (below) |

Each entry in `checks`:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | Check name |
| `type` | string | Check type |
| `params` | object | The check's parameters after normalization |
| `passed` | boolean | Result |
| `detail` | string | Human-readable result, for example `3 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted` |
| `attempts` | integer | Number of samples taken |
| `duration_s` | number | Seconds spent on the check |
| `started` | string | UTC timestamp |
| `history` | array | Every sample (last 50): `t` (seconds since start), `passed`, `detail`, and `unready: true` on a failing sample where the node gave no usable state |
| `evidence` | array | Raw commands from the final sample: `node`, `cmd`, `rc`, `output`, `stderr` |

Long outputs are truncated (the last 20,000 characters of command output are kept).

### Markdown

`--markdown FILE` writes a short summary: a heading (passed, failed, inconclusive, or could not run), the reason when inconclusive, the pass/fail counts and lab name, a table of checks with failures first, and a footer with the Netdryrun and containerlab versions. This is the same text appended to the GitHub Actions step summary.

### JUnit XML

`--junit FILE` writes one `<testsuite name="netdryrun">` with one `<testcase>` per check:

- `classname` is `netdryrun.<type>`, for example `netdryrun.route`
- a failed check has a `<failure>` whose `message` is the detail and whose body is the evidence as JSON
- in an `inconclusive` run, failed checks have an `<error>` instead of a `<failure>` (they could not run meaningfully), and they count as `errors`, not `failures`
- a lab error adds a testcase named `lab` with an `<error>` element


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/github-action/

# GitHub Action

The action installs containerlab, installs Netdryrun™, runs your checks, writes a summary to the job page, uploads the JSON and JUnit reports as an artifact, and fails the job if any check fails.

```yaml title=".github/workflows/network-dryrun.yml"
name: Network dry run
on: pull_request
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.0
        with:
          path: network/        # folder containing netdryrun.yml
```

It needs a Linux runner with Docker. GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners work.

## Inputs

| Input | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `path` | `.` | `netdryrun.yml` or the folder containing it |
| `containerlab-version` | `0.81.1` | containerlab version to install, pinned for reproducible runs. Empty means latest. If containerlab is already installed, it is used as is, with a warning if the version differs. |
| `json-report` | `netdryrun-report.json` | Path for the JSON evidence report |
| `junit-report` | `netdryrun-junit.xml` | Path for the JUnit XML report |
| `upload-artifact` | `true` | Upload the reports as a workflow artifact |
| `artifact-name` | `netdryrun-report` | Name of the uploaded artifact |
| `settle` | `10` | Seconds to wait before post-convergence checks |
| `hold` | `10` | Seconds a post-convergence check must hold |
| `pr-comment` | `false` | On pull requests, post one comment with the verdict, failures first, and the evidence for each failed check. Updated in place on every push. Needs `permissions: pull-requests: write` |
| `github-token` | `${{ github.token }}` | Token used for the PR comment |
| `cloud` | `false` | Upload the evidence to Netdryrun Cloud (beta). Needs `permissions: id-token: write`; no secrets are configured |
| `cloud-url` | `https://cloud.netdryrun.com` | Netdryrun Cloud address |

## Outputs

| Output | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `status` | `passed`, `failed`, `error` or `inconclusive` (the lab never reached a testable state, so the run says nothing about the change; the job still fails) |
| `inconclusive-reason` | Why the run was inconclusive; empty otherwise |
| `passed` | Number of passed checks |
| `failed` | Number of failed checks |
| `evidence-url` | Link to the evidence page, when `cloud` is `true` |

## Examples

### Only run when network files change

```yaml
name: Network dry run
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "network/**"
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.0
        with:
          path: network/
```

### Use the outputs in a later step

```yaml
      - uses: netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.0
        id: ndr
        with:
          path: network/
      - if: always()
        run: echo "Netdryrun ${{ steps.ndr.outputs.status }}: ${{ steps.ndr.outputs.passed }} passed, ${{ steps.ndr.outputs.failed }} failed"
```

### Several labs

```yaml
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        lab: [network/core, network/edge]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.0
        with:
          path: ${{ matrix.lab }}
          artifact-name: netdryrun-${{ strategy.job-index }}
```

Give each matrix job its own `artifact-name`; artifact names must be unique within a workflow run.

### Comment the verdict on every pull request

```yaml
name: Network dry run
on: pull_request
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.0
        with:
          path: network/
          pr-comment: true
```

## Security notes

- **A lab is code that runs as root on the runner.** containerlab starts privileged containers with access to the host. Netdryrun passes the lab process a minimal environment (no job tokens, not the runner user's home directory), but that only narrows exposure; it is not a security boundary.
- **Run labs from untrusted pull requests (forks) only in jobs with no secrets**, a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and without `id-token: write`. Never run them under `pull_request_target`.
- `pr-comment` needs `pull-requests: write`; `cloud` needs `id-token: write`. Grant each only when you use it.
- Uploaded report artifacts contain raw command output from the lab and are kept for 14 days. Don't put real secrets in lab configs.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/ai-agents/

# AI agents (MCP server)

AI agents are starting to change networks. Netdryrun™ includes an [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server that gives an agent a safety gate: it dry-runs the proposed change in a real lab and proceeds only if every check passes.

## Set up the MCP server

```bash
pip install netdryrun
```

The MCP server is built in: `netdryrun mcp` starts it over stdio. The same requirements apply as for the CLI: Linux or WSL2, Docker, containerlab. The server runs labs on the machine where it runs.

### Claude Code

On Linux or inside WSL:

```bash
claude mcp add netdryrun -- netdryrun mcp
```

Add `-s project` to write the server into `.mcp.json` in the current folder, so everyone who works in that repository gets it.

On Windows, with Claude Code running on Windows and Netdryrun installed in WSL, start the server through `wsl.exe` and give the full path to `netdryrun` inside WSL:

```text
$ claude mcp add -s project netdryrun -- wsl.exe -d Ubuntu-22.04 -- /home/dmin/ndr-docs/bin/netdryrun mcp
Added stdio MCP server netdryrun with command: wsl.exe -d Ubuntu-22.04 -- /home/dmin/ndr-docs/bin/netdryrun mcp to project config
$ claude mcp get netdryrun
netdryrun:
  Scope: Project config (shared via .mcp.json)
  Status: ✓ Connected
  Type: stdio
  Command: wsl.exe
  Args: -d Ubuntu-22.04 -- /home/dmin/ndr-docs/bin/netdryrun mcp
```

(Claude Code 2.1.116. Use your own distribution name and path; `which netdryrun` inside WSL prints it.)

`dry_run` takes 30 seconds to several minutes. Start Claude Code with a longer tool timeout, in milliseconds, so it does not give up first:

```bash
MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT=600000 claude
```

See [MCP tool calls time out](troubleshooting.md#mcp-tool-calls-time-out-in-the-client).

### Other MCP clients

Configure a stdio server with command `netdryrun` and argument `mcp`. Most clients take JSON like this (this is the `.mcp.json` Claude Code wrote above, with the Linux command):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "netdryrun": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "netdryrun",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Without installing, use `"command": "uvx", "args": ["netdryrun", "mcp"]`. On Windows, use the `wsl.exe` command and arguments shown above. Set the client's tool-call timeout to at least 5 minutes.

## Workflow

1. The agent writes its proposed change into the lab's configs (in a lab folder with a containerlab topology and a `netdryrun.yml`).
2. It calls `dry_run` on that folder.
3. It applies the change elsewhere only if `status` is `passed`.

## Demo: a ticket, a tempting change, a verdict


[`examples/agent-demo`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/agent-demo): the customer's new block must reach the upstream and the peer. The tempting change, removing the prefix-list filters, passes every ticket check, session check and ping, but leaks upstream routes and the upstream's default route to the peer, and accepts a prefix the customer doesn't own. The network team's leak guards fail, so the verdict is `DO NOT APPLY THIS CHANGE`. The proper fix, two prefix-list lines, passes the same checks. The checks never change; only the config does. Both attempts are a scripted replay (hand-written diffs, not output from a real agent); `demo.sh` runs them, and CI runs it on pushes to `main` and on pull requests. In a [real run](#a-real-agent-run), a fresh Claude Code agent with only the ticket, the lab and these MCP tools made the correct two-line change on the first try and proposed it with a `passed` verdict.

## Give the agent a ticket (the TICKET.md pattern)

An agent does better with a written task and explicit rules than with a chat message. Put a `TICKET.md` in the lab folder, next to `topology.clab.yml`, `configs/` and `netdryrun.yml`. [`examples/agent-demo/TICKET.md`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/examples/agent-demo/TICKET.md) is a complete example. A ticket says:

- **The goal, in network terms.** "The customer's new block 10.101.0.0/24 must reach the upstream and the peer." Name the routers, ASes and prefixes.
- **What the agent may change.** "Change only `configs/edge1.conf`." A small allowed surface makes the change easy to review.
- **What it must not change.** "Don't edit `netdryrun.yml`." The checks belong to the network team. An agent that may edit the checks can make any change pass.
- **The gate.** "Before proposing the change, run Netdryrun on this folder (`netdryrun run <folder>`, or the `dry_run` MCP tool) and include the verdict. Propose it only if the status is `passed`."

Then the prompt can stay short. The real run below used: "Work the ticket in TICKET.md in the current folder, following its rules", plus the path the MCP tools use for the folder and a request for the diff and the verdict at the end. Nothing about the solution.

More guidance for the prompt or the agent's instructions file:

- Ask for the verdict and the names of any failed checks in the final answer, so a human can review the evidence instead of the agent's reasoning.
- Tell it what to do on a failure: read `detail` for each failed check, fix the config, run again. Never weaken or delete a check; if it thinks a check is wrong, it should say so and stop.
- Don't show it the answer. In `examples/agent-demo`, the README, `changes/` and `demo.sh` contain the solution, so the real run could only see `TICKET.md`, `netdryrun.yml`, `topology.clab.yml` and `configs/`.
- A pass covers only the checks that exist. Give the agent the network team's standing guards (leak checks, `present: false` routes), not only the ticket's acceptance checks.

The repository's [`AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/AGENTS.md) has the same rules written for agents.

## A real agent run

[`AGENT-RUN.md`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/examples/agent-demo/AGENT-RUN.md) records one real run on `examples/agent-demo`, not the scripted replay:

- **Agent:** Claude Code 2.1.116 in headless mode (`claude -p`). It could read and edit files and call the Netdryrun MCP tools. No shell, no web access, so its only way to test was Netdryrun.
- **What it did:** read the ticket, the router config and `netdryrun.yml`; added the new block to the two prefix lists in `configs/edge1.conf`; called `dry_run`; got `status: passed`, 14 of 14 checks, verdict `SAFE TO PROCEED`; proposed the two-line change with the verdict. 7 turns, 69 seconds.
- **Checked afterwards:** it changed only `configs/edge1.conf`, and a fresh `netdryrun run` on its folder gave `PASSED: 14 passed, 0 failed`.

The agent did not make the tempting leaky change, so this run did not show Netdryrun catching a mistake (`demo.sh` shows that). It shows the workflow end to end: the agent found the tool, ran the network team's checks through MCP, and its proposal came with a verdict from a real lab. It is one run of one model on one ticket.

## Gate agent-made pull requests in CI

An agent's own `dry_run` is a claim. Run the same checks again in CI, where the agent cannot change the result:

```yaml title=".github/workflows/network-dryrun.yml"
name: Network dry run
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "network/**"
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.0
        with:
          path: network/
          pr-comment: true
```

Then, in the repository settings:

- **Make the job a required status check** on the default branch, so a failed verdict blocks the merge.
- **Protect the checks.** Add a `CODEOWNERS` line such as `network/netdryrun.yml @your-org/network-team` and require code-owner review. A PR that edits the checks then needs a human from the network team, while config-only PRs need only the green check and a normal review.
- **Keep agent PRs away from secrets.** The lab runs as root on the runner. Follow the [Action security notes](github-action.md#security-notes): no secrets in the job, no `pull_request_target`.

The PR comment lists failures first with their evidence, so the reviewer sees what the lab saw. See [GitHub Action](github-action.md) for every input.

## Tools

The server has these tools: `dry_run`, `run_checks`, `record_baseline`, `validate` and `check_types`.


| Tool | Arguments | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `dry_run` | `path`, `keep_lab` (default `false`) | Deploy the lab, run every check, destroy the lab, return the verdict. Takes 1 to 5 minutes. |
| `run_checks` | `path` | Run the checks against a lab that is already running (no deploy or destroy) |
| `record_baseline` | `topology`, `deploy` (default `true`), `wait_seconds` (default `45`) | Deploy the lab, snapshot its BGP sessions, prefix counts and routes as `netdryrun.yml` text, destroy the lab. Returns the YAML; nothing is written to disk. Like [`netdryrun record`](reference/cli.md#record) |
| `validate` | `path` | Validate `netdryrun.yml` without starting a lab |
| `check_types` | | List supported check types and their keys, to help write `netdryrun.yml` |

The server also exposes the last full JSON report as a resource, `netdryrun://report/{path}`.

## Result and verdict

`dry_run` and `run_checks` return JSON like this:

```json
{
  "status": "failed",
  "passed": 5,
  "failed": 1,
  "error": null,
  "lab": "ndr-frr-broken",
  "checks": [
    {"name": "r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent", "passed": false,
     "detail": "unexpectedly present via bgp (not selected)"}
  ],
  "evidence_file": "/path/to/lab/netdryrun-report.json",
  "verdict": "DO NOT APPLY THIS CHANGE"
}
```

(`checks` is shortened here; the real result lists every check.)

`verdict` is a separate field with one of three values:

- `SAFE TO PROCEED` when `status` is `passed`
- `DO NOT APPLY THIS CHANGE` for `failed` or `error`, including config errors
- `INCONCLUSIVE: the lab did not reach a testable state; this says nothing about your change. Do not apply it until a run passes.` when `status` is `inconclusive`: the lab never came up far enough for the checks to mean anything ([rules](reference/cli.md#when-a-run-is-inconclusive)). `inconclusive_reason` says what was seen. Rerun it, perhaps with a longer `timeout`; don't rewrite the change because of it.

Tell the agent what to do with each verdict: propose the change only on `SAFE TO PROCEED`; on `DO NOT APPLY THIS CHANGE`, read the failed checks, fix the config and run again; on `INCONCLUSIVE`, rerun, and if it stays inconclusive, report that the lab does not come up instead of changing the config. [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#inconclusive-the-lab-never-came-up) shows a real inconclusive run.

The full evidence is written to `netdryrun-report.json` next to `netdryrun.yml`.

## Safety model

- **It never touches production.** The server has no tool that pushes config anywhere. It only builds and tests labs.
- **No raw device output in tool results.** Tool results contain normalized check results (name, pass/fail, a short detail), not raw device output. Text inside a lab, such as a banner or a route description, cannot inject instructions into the agent through the tool result. Raw evidence goes to the JSON report file.
- **Labs are code.** containerlab runs privileged containers. Only point the server at topologies you trust, on a machine you would let run Docker.

A pass is evidence from a lab, not a guarantee about production. See [what a lab cannot prove](trust.md#what-a-lab-cannot-prove).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/troubleshooting/

# Troubleshooting

Each error below was reproduced on purpose on WSL2 (Ubuntu 22.04) with containerlab 0.81.1, using Netdryrun™ 0.2.0, and 0.3.0 for the inconclusive case. The output is copied from those runs. Rerun on 0.3.0, the missing-containerlab and unknown-node errors print the same messages.

Exit code `2` means the run could not complete (a config error or a lab error). Exit code `1` means a check failed. See [exit codes](reference/cli.md#exit-codes).

## containerlab is not installed

```text
$ netdryrun run my-lab
Netdryrun 0.2.0: 14 checks from my-lab/netdryrun.yml
Destroying lab...
warning: lab cleanup failed: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'containerlab'
ERROR: 'containerlab' not found on PATH
```

Exit code `2`. Netdryrun drives the `containerlab` CLI and needs it on `PATH`. Install it ([containerlab.dev/install](https://containerlab.dev/install/)) and check with `containerlab version`. The same error names `docker` if Docker is missing. The cleanup warning is harmless: nothing was deployed.

## Docker or containerlab permission denied

As a user who is not in the `docker` and `clab_admins` groups:

```text
$ netdryrun run my-lab
Netdryrun 0.2.0: 14 checks from my-lab/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab my-lab (3 nodes)...
Destroying lab...
warning: lab cleanup failed: ROR
...
ERROR: containerlab deploy failed:

   ERROR

  User 'ndrtest' is not part of containerlab admin group 'clab_admins', which is required to execute this command.
  To add yourself to this group, run the following command:
      $ sudo usermod -aG clab_admins ndrtest.
```

```text
$ docker ps
permission denied while trying to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock
```

Fix: add your user to both groups, then start a new login session so the groups apply.

```bash
sudo usermod -aG docker,clab_admins "$USER"
```

On WSL, close the terminal and run `wsl --shutdown` from Windows, then open it again. Check with `id`: both groups must be listed.

```text
$ id
uid=1001(ndrtest) gid=1001(ndrtest) groups=1001(ndrtest),998(clab_admins),999(docker)
```

After this, the same user deployed and ran the lab. Running Netdryrun with `sudo` also works, but then the reports are owned by root.

## A check names a node that is not in the topology

`netdryrun validate` checks the file's syntax and values, not the node names against the topology. A typo (`r9` instead of `r1`) passes validation:

```text
$ netdryrun validate unk
OK: unk/netdryrun.yml (14 checks, lab /home/dmin/ndr-docs/unk/topology.clab.yml)
  - [bgp_session] r9: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established
  ...
```

`run` catches it before anything is deployed:

```text
$ netdryrun run unk
Netdryrun 0.2.0: 14 checks from unk/netdryrun.yml
Destroying lab...
ERROR: unknown node(s) r9; the topology has r1, r2, r3
```

Exit code `2`. Use the node names from the topology's `nodes:` section (`r1`), not the container names (`clab-my-lab-r1`).

## The lab never converges (timeout)

A positive check waits up to `timeout` seconds (default 120) for the network to converge, then fails. Here r1 has the wrong `remote-as` for r2 and `timeout` is 30:

```text
$ netdryrun run slow
Netdryrun 0.2.0: 14 checks from slow/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndrdocs-slow (3 nodes)...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established -- state is established (13.8s)
  ...
  [FAIL] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is idle (30.1s)
  [FAIL] r2: BGP session to 10.0.12.1 is established -- state is idle (30.1s)
  [FAIL] r1: route 192.168.33.0/24 via bgp is present -- not active via bgp; seen: nothing (30.1s)
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [FAIL] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 2 and <= 10 -- session is idle; prefix counts are only meaningful when established (30.4s)
  ...
Destroying lab...
FAILED: 10 passed, 4 failed (14 checks)
```

A check that fails at exactly its timeout (`30.1s` here) never reached the expected state. Two causes:

- **The change really breaks something.** The `detail` says what the router reported (`state is idle`). This is the test working.
- **The lab is slow to boot.** SR Linux, SONiC and cEOS take longer than FRR. Raise `timeout` at the top of `netdryrun.yml`, or on one check. `examples/srl-frr` uses 120.

To see why, keep the lab and look inside:

```text
$ netdryrun run slow --keep-on-failure
...
Lab ndrdocs-slow left running for debugging; destroy with: containerlab destroy -t /home/dmin/ndr-docs/slow/topology.clab.yml --cleanup
FAILED: 10 passed, 4 failed (14 checks)
$ docker exec clab-ndrdocs-slow-r1 vtysh -c "show bgp summary"
...
Neighbor        V         AS   MsgRcvd   MsgSent   TblVer  InQ OutQ  Up/Down State/PfxRcd   PfxSnt Desc
10.0.12.2       4      65099         6        12        0    0    0    never         Idle        0 N/A
r3(10.0.13.2)   4      65003        38        40        3    0    0 00:01:17            2        3 FRRouting/10.4.1_git
```

r1 expects AS 65099 at 10.0.12.2, but r2 is AS 65002. Destroy the lab with the command Netdryrun printed.

## SR Linux fails on a Windows drive (/mnt/c)

On WSL, files under `/mnt/c` are on the Windows filesystem, which has no Linux permissions. If containerlab's lab directory is there, SR Linux cannot save its config. Running containerlab directly in such a folder:

```text
$ containerlab deploy -t topology.clab.yml
11:07:03 INFO Creating lab directory path=/mnt/c/Users/.../srlmnt/clab-ndrdocs-srlmnt
11:07:03 INFO unable to adjust Labdir file ACLs: operation not supported
...
11:07:32 ERRO node "srl1" post-deploy: command execution error:Error in /system:
    Setting permissions for file '/etc/opt/srlinux/config.tmp' failed with error_code = 1 [Operation not permitted]
Error: Commit failed
```

The SR Linux container keeps running, but without its startup config, so every check fails:

```text
  [FAIL] srl1: BGP session to 10.0.100.2 is established -- neighbor 10.0.100.2 not configured (seen: none) (122.6s)
```

Netdryrun avoids this. When the topology is under `/mnt/`, it puts containerlab's lab directory in `~/.cache/netdryrun/labs` (unless you set `CLAB_LABDIR_BASE` yourself). The same folder with `netdryrun run .`:

```text
$ netdryrun run .
Netdryrun 0.2.0: 6 checks from netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndrdocs-srlmnt (2 nodes)...
  [PASS] srl1: BGP session to 10.0.100.2 is established -- state is established (31.2s)
  ...
PASSED: 6 passed, 0 failed (6 checks)
```

If you deploy with containerlab yourself (for example for `netdryrun check`), either keep the lab on the Linux filesystem (`~/...`) or set `CLAB_LABDIR_BASE` to a Linux path. Keeping labs on the Linux filesystem is also faster.

## The cEOS image is missing

Arista does not allow cEOS to be redistributed, so you import it yourself. If the image named in the topology is not in Docker, Docker tries to pull it from Docker Hub and fails:

```text
$ netdryrun run ceos
Netdryrun 0.2.0: 7 checks from ceos/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndrdocs-ceos (2 nodes)...
Destroying lab...
ERROR: containerlab deploy failed:
10:57:23 INFO Containerlab started version=0.81.1
10:57:23 INFO Parsing & checking topology file=topology.clab.yml
10:57:23 INFO Removing directory path=/home/dmin/ndr-docs/ceos/clab-ndrdocs-ceos
10:57:23 INFO Pulling image image=docker.io/library/ceos:4.34.1F
10:57:25 ERRO Failed to pull image image=docker.io/library/ceos:4.34.1F err="Error response from daemon: pull access denied for ceos, repository does not exist or may require 'docker login'"
```

Fix: download cEOS-lab from arista.com (free account) and import it with the exact name and tag the topology uses: `docker import cEOS-lab-<version>.tar ceos:<version>`, as the comment in `examples/arista-frr/topology.clab.yml` says. Then check that Docker has it:

```text
$ docker images ceos
IMAGE          ID             DISK USAGE   CONTENT SIZE   EXTRA
ceos:4.36.3M   94cc1e5462fe       3.55GB          976MB   U
```

`examples/arista-frr` expects `ceos:4.36.3M`. Either import with that tag or change `image:` in the topology to match yours.

## Two labs with the same name

containerlab lab names are global on a machine: containers are named `clab-<lab>-<node>`. Netdryrun deploys with `containerlab deploy --reconfigure`, so a second lab with the same `name:` **replaces** the first one, even from a different folder. Here `my-lab` was left running with `--keep`, then a copy of it in `other-lab` (same `name: my-lab`) was run:

```text
$ netdryrun run other-lab
Netdryrun 0.2.0: 14 checks from other-lab/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab my-lab (3 nodes)...
...
Destroying lab...
```

The first lab is gone:

```text
$ netdryrun check my-lab
Netdryrun 0.2.0: 14 checks from my-lab/netdryrun.yml
ERROR: lab containers not running: clab-my-lab-r1, clab-my-lab-r2, clab-my-lab-r3
```

Fix: give every lab a unique `name:`. Before you run, check what is up with `docker ps` or `containerlab inspect --all`. On a shared CI runner or machine, put something unique in the name (for example the branch).

## A host port is already in use

If a topology publishes ports on the host (`ports:` on a node), two labs cannot use the same host port:

```text
$ netdryrun run p2
Netdryrun 0.2.0: 14 checks from p2/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndrdocs-p2 (3 nodes)...
Destroying lab...
ERROR: containerlab deploy failed:
...
11:05:40 ERRO node "r1" deploy: Error response from daemon: failed to set up container networking: driver failed programming external connectivity on endpoint clab-ndrdocs-p2-r1 (40a6a46a...): Bind for 0.0.0.0:18179 failed: port is already allocated
```

Fix: Netdryrun does not need published ports; it runs every command with `docker exec`. Remove `ports:` from the topology, or use different host ports per lab. `docker ps` shows which container holds the port.

## link_down on an SR Linux node

Failure scenarios take links down with `ip link` inside the node, which works on FRR, SONiC and cEOS but not yet on SR Linux. `validate` accepts the file; the error comes when the scenario starts, after the main checks:

```text
$ netdryrun run srl-ld
Netdryrun 0.2.0: 6 checks from srl-ld/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndrdocs-srlld (2 nodes)...
  [PASS] srl1: BGP session to 10.0.100.2 is established -- state is established (16.1s)
  ...
  [PASS] frr1: ping 192.168.10.1 from 192.168.20.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (need 2) (21.5s)
Scenario: srl1-frr1 link fails
Destroying lab...
ERROR: failure scenarios on SR Linux nodes (srl1) are not supported yet; take the link down on the FRR/Linux side of the link instead
```

Fix: take down the other end of the same link. For `examples/srl-frr`, the link is `srl1:e1-1` to `frr1:eth1`:

```yaml
scenarios:
  - name: srl1-frr1 link fails
    link_down: {node: frr1, interface: eth1}
```

The effect on the network is the same: the link is down for both sides. `node_isolated` on an SR Linux node fails the same way; isolate its neighbors' links instead.

## MCP tool calls time out in the client

`dry_run` deploys a lab, so it takes 30 seconds to several minutes. Many MCP clients give up on a tool call sooner. Reproduced with the Python MCP SDK (mcp 2.3.0) and a 20-second client timeout:

```text
MCPError: Request 'tools/call' timed out
after 20.0s
```

With a 300-second timeout, the same call returned the full result after 143 seconds.

When the client gives up, it usually stops the server, and **the lab is left running**. Right after the timeout above:

```text
$ docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Status}}'
clab-my-lab-r1 Up 27 seconds
clab-my-lab-r2 Up 27 seconds
clab-my-lab-r3 Up 27 seconds
```

The next `dry_run` on the same folder redeploys over it and cleans up, or destroy it yourself with `containerlab destroy -t my-lab/topology.clab.yml --cleanup`.

Fixes:

- **Raise the client's tool timeout** to at least 5 minutes. In Claude Code, set `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT` (milliseconds) before starting it, for example `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT=600000 claude`. For other clients, look for a tool-call or request timeout setting.
- **Make the lab faster.** Lower `timeout` in `netdryrun.yml` so a broken change fails sooner, and pull images in advance so the first call does not wait on a download.
- **If the client cannot wait that long**, let the agent run `netdryrun run <folder>` in a shell and read `netdryrun-report.json`.

## Inconclusive: the lab never came up

Exit code `3` means checks failed, but the lab never reached a testable state, so the result says nothing about your change. Reproduced with Netdryrun 0.3.0 by turning off `bgpd` in the FRR `daemons` file of a copy of `examples/frr-bgp` (and `timeout: 30`):

```text
$ netdryrun run . --json report.json
Netdryrun 0.3.0: 7 checks from netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndrdocs-nobgp (3 nodes)...
  [FAIL] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- error: `vtysh -c show bgp neighbors json` failed on r1 (rc=1): bgpd is not running (33.1s)
  [FAIL] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established -- error: `vtysh -c show bgp neighbors json` failed on r1 (rc=1): bgpd is not running (33.1s)
  [FAIL] r1: route 192.168.3.0/24 via bgp is present -- not active via bgp; seen: nothing (33.1s)
  [FAIL] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 0/3 replies (need 2) (33.1s)
  [FAIL] r1: BGP best path for 192.168.2.0/24 has as-path '65002', next hop 10.0.12.2 -- error: `vtysh -c show bgp ipv4 unicast 192.168.2.0/24 json` failed on r1 (rc=1): bgpd is not running (33.1s)
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [FAIL] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 1 and <= 10 -- error: `vtysh -c show bgp neighbors json` failed on r1 (rc=1): bgpd is not running (30.1s)
  [PASS] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- absent (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.1s)
Destroying lab...
INCONCLUSIVE: the lab did not reach a testable state: r1 never returned usable BGP state (r1: error: `vtysh -c show bgp neighbors json` failed on r1 (rc=1): bgpd is not running), and no check passed on any sample. Rerun with a longer timeout, or check that the lab boots (6 of 7 checks failed; this says nothing about the change)
  wrote json report: report.json
```

The JSON report has the same text in `inconclusive_reason`, and every unready sample in `history` is marked:

```json
{"t": 33.1, "passed": false, "detail": "error: `vtysh -c show bgp neighbors json` failed on r1 (rc=1): bgpd is not running", "unready": true}
```

How it differs from the other results:

- **`error` (exit `2`):** the run could not start or finish: a config error, a missing tool, a failed deploy.
- **`failed` (exit `1`):** the lab was up and something is wrong. A configured BGP session that is down (an ASN typo, as in [the lab never converges](#the-lab-never-converges-timeout)) is `failed`, not `inconclusive`.
- **`inconclusive` (exit `3`):** no positive check passed on any sample, and every failed check is on a node whose CLI or BGP never answered.

Fix: check that the lab boots (`containerlab inspect`, `docker logs <container>`), that the routing daemon is enabled, and that `timeout` is long enough for slow NOSes, then rerun. One known limit: a change that deletes a node's whole BGP config looks the same and is reported `inconclusive`. It is still never `passed`. See the [full rules](reference/cli.md#when-a-run-is-inconclusive).

## Still stuck

Run with `--keep-on-failure`, look inside the nodes with `docker exec`, and read the JSON report (`--json report.json`): every check keeps the raw commands and output. If it looks like a bug, [open an issue](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues) with the report attached. See [Support](support.md).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/faq/

# FAQ

## Does Netdryrun touch my production network?

No. Netdryrun™ only builds labs with containerlab on the machine where it runs, runs read-only commands inside the lab containers (with `docker exec`), and destroys the lab. It has no command, option or MCP tool that connects to a real device or pushes config anywhere. You apply the change to production yourself, with your normal process, after the test passes.

## What does a pass prove?

A pass means every check in your `netdryrun.yml` held in a lab running real routing software: positive checks reached the expected state within the timeout, and negative checks held for the hold time after convergence. It is strong evidence that the change does what you intended at the protocol and policy level.

It does not prove:

- **anything you did not check.** A pass covers the checks that exist. A leak with no negative check for it passes.
- **vendor or version behavior.** FRR, SR Linux, SONiC VS and cEOS are not your production routers or images.
- **scale, hardware or timing.** A lab has a few nodes and small tables, no ASICs, and different convergence times.

See [what a lab cannot prove](trust.md#what-a-lab-cannot-prove). The [verdict corpus](corpus.md) shows where Netdryrun was right and wrong on 30 realistic changes.

## What does "inconclusive" mean?

A run is `inconclusive` (exit code `3`) when checks failed but the lab never reached a state where they mean anything, for example a node whose BGP daemon never started. It says nothing about the change, good or bad: rerun, raise `timeout`, or check that the lab boots. Don't change the network change because of it, and don't apply it either: only `passed` means go.

The rules are conservative. A configured session that is down, a missing route or a failed ping is always `failed`, because an ASN typo looks exactly like a slow lab from the outside. See [when a run is inconclusive](reference/cli.md#when-a-run-is-inconclusive) and [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#inconclusive-the-lab-never-came-up).

## How is it different from Batfish, pyATS or netlab?

- **Batfish** models configs without booting anything. It is fast, covers many vendors and large networks, and answers broad questions. Netdryrun runs the real routing software, so it sees what the implementation actually does, on fewer nodes.
- **pyATS / Genie** is a full Python test framework with many parsers, for labs and production devices. Netdryrun is a YAML file of checks and a CLI, aimed at one job: a pass/fail gate in CI.
- **netlab** builds labs from a short topology description and has its own validation tests. Netdryrun takes a containerlab topology you already have, including one netlab generated.

They work together. See [When to use what](when-to-use-what.md) for a longer, neutral comparison.

## Which network operating systems are supported?

FRR, Nokia SR Linux, SONiC (docker-sonic-vs) and Arista EOS (cEOS, bring your own image). Labs can mix them: the examples pair each one with FRR. See [drivers](reference/config.md#drivers) for what each driver supports.

## Why not Cisco or Juniper?

Their lab images are licensed. Netdryrun's CI and examples must run for anyone, so every image they use has to be free to pull: FRR, SR Linux and SONiC VS are. Arista cEOS is free to download with an account but can't be redistributed, so its example needs you to import your own image.

Cisco and Juniper images (for example IOS XRd, Cisco 8000 emulator, cRPD, vJunos) need an account, a license or both, and several are virtual machines that containerlab runs through vrnetlab. Drivers for them are on the roadmap, following the same bring-your-own-image model as cEOS. If you need one, say so in an [issue](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues).

## Does it work on Windows?

Yes, through WSL2. containerlab needs Linux, so install Docker and containerlab inside a WSL2 distribution (Ubuntu 22.04 is what we test on) and run Netdryrun there. Keep labs on the Linux filesystem (`~/...`) rather than under `/mnt/c`: it is faster, and SR Linux cannot save its config on a Windows drive. Netdryrun works around the second problem; see [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#sr-linux-fails-on-a-windows-drive-mntc). All the outputs in this documentation were produced on WSL2.

## How much memory and CPU does it need?

Memory used per node once the lab is up, measured with `docker stats` on WSL2 (20 cores, 16 GB):

| Node | Image | Memory |
|---|---|---|
| FRR | `quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1` | 23 to 25 MiB |
| SONiC VS | `docker-sonic-vs:latest` | 302 MiB |
| Arista cEOS | `ceos:4.36.3M` | 903 MiB |
| Nokia SR Linux | `ghcr.io/nokia/srlinux:26.7.2` | 1.9 GB (1,947,377,664 bytes, read from the container's cgroup `memory.current`, because `docker stats` shows 0 for SR Linux) |

CPU is busy only while nodes boot. Once up, FRR and SONiC used about 1% of one core or less; cEOS was using about one full core when measured, shortly after boot.

Plan for the sum of your nodes plus a few hundred MB for Docker and containerlab. A small FRR lab runs on any laptop. A lab with several SR Linux or cEOS nodes needs a machine with 8 GB or more. GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners have enough memory for every example.

## How long does a run take, and what does CI cost?

On GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners, measured from three CI runs on `main` on 2026-10-27, before 0.3.0 added a few checks per example:

| CI job | What it does | Time |
|---|---|---|
| `e2e (frr-bgp)` | Install containerlab and Netdryrun, pull FRR, run the checks and a link-failure scenario | 100 to 107 s |
| `e2e (srl-frr)` | The same with SR Linux and FRR (the SR Linux image is 3.2 GB) | 88 to 107 s |
| `catches-bad-change` | Run `frr-bgp-broken` and expect it to fail | 54 to 66 s |
| `agent-demo` | Replay the agent demo: two full runs | 82 to 94 s |

The whole CI workflow, with these jobs in parallel, took 2 minutes 10 seconds to 2 minutes 38 seconds in the last ten successful runs.

GitHub Actions minutes are free on public repositories with standard GitHub-hosted runners. On private repositories, each job uses minutes from your plan, rounded up to the whole minute, so a job like `e2e (frr-bgp)` uses 2 minutes. See [GitHub's billing page](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/managing-billing-for-your-products/managing-billing-for-github-actions/about-billing-for-github-actions) for current prices. Netdryrun itself is free.

Local runs are faster once images are pulled; see the times on the [examples page](examples.md).

## Does it collect any data?

No. The CLI, the GitHub Action and the MCP server have no telemetry and don't phone home. Reports are written only to the files you ask for. The one exception is opt-in: `cloud: true` on the GitHub Action uploads the JSON report to Netdryrun Cloud. See [privacy](trust.md#privacy) and the [privacy notice](privacy.md).

## What is the license?

Apache-2.0, for the code. "Netdryrun" and the logo are trademarks: forks are welcome under a different name. See [Trust and security](trust.md#license).

## Where do I get help?

Read [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md) first. Then [open an issue](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues) with the JSON report attached. See [Support](support.md).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/corpus/

# Network Change Verdict Corpus

How much does a typical "ping after the change" test miss? This corpus answers that with data anyone can rerun.

## Method

- **The network:** a small provider (AS65000, two routers) with a customer, an upstream transit and a settlement-free peer, running FRR in containerlab. Its written intent is in [INTENT.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/INTENT.md).
- **The changes:** 30 realistic edits ([cases](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/corpus/cases)): route leaks, filter typos, mass withdrawals, fat-fingered ASNs, latent risks, and safe changes that must not be blocked.
- **Pre-registered verdicts:** each case's expected verdict (would an experienced operator reject it?) was **committed to git before any run**. Verdicts are never edited afterwards; findings after the run are listed separately below.
- **Three strategies, same running lab per case:**
    1. **Ping only:** the customer pings the upstream and the peer.
    2. **All BGP sessions up:** every session established.
    3. **Netdryrun™ intent checks:** one [intent spec](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/specs/intent.yml), written once and used unchanged for every case, so it can't be tuned to win.
- **Rerun it:** `python corpus/run.py` on any Linux or WSL2 machine with Docker and containerlab.
- **Rerun it on GitHub's machines:** fork the repository, then run the [Reproduce corpus](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/reproduce-corpus.yml) workflow from your fork's Actions tab. It installs containerlab 0.81.1 and Netdryrun on a GitHub-hosted runner, runs every case, uploads `results.json`, `RESULTS.md` and the run log as artifacts, and lists every verdict that differs from the committed [`results.json`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/results/results.json) in the run summary.

## Results



Generated 2026-10-26T21:43:03+00:00 with netdryrun 0.2.0, containerlab 0.81.1, FRR quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1, commit `ec23379`. Rerun everything with `python corpus/run.py`.

**Conflict of interest:** the Netdryrun maintainers wrote this corpus and the runner. Expected verdicts were committed before any run (see the git history of [`corpus/cases/`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/corpus/cases)). Losses are kept and shown at the same size as the catches.

## Summary (30 cases: 19 harmful, 11 safe)

| Strategy | Correct | Harmful changes caught | Approved a bad change | Blocked a good change | Errors |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ping only | **20/30** | 9/19 | 10 | 0 | 0 |
| All BGP sessions up | **15/30** | 4/19 | 15 | 0 | 0 |
| Netdryrun intent checks | **24/30** | 14/19 | 5 | 1 | 0 |

## Every case

| Case | Category | Expected | Ping only | Sessions up | Netdryrun | What Netdryrun flagged |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `01-no-change` [No change (control)](corpus/01-no-change.md) | control | safe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | nothing |
| `02-med-to-upstream` [Set MED on routes sent to the upstream](corpus/02-med-to-upstream.md) | traffic-engineering | safe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | nothing |
| `03-prepend-to-peer` [Prepend our AS twice toward the peer](corpus/03-prepend-to-peer.md) | traffic-engineering | safe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | nothing |
| `04-tag-community-upstream` [Tag our aggregate with an informational community toward the upstream](corpus/04-tag-community-upstream.md) | hygiene | safe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | nothing |
| `05-description-only` [Change an interface description](corpus/05-description-only.md) | hygiene | safe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | nothing |
| `06-customer-adds-prefix` [Customer announces a second allowed /24](corpus/06-customer-adds-prefix.md) | customer-growth | safe | ✅ | ✅ | ⚠️ blocked a good change | I5 upstream receives exactly our 2 prefixes; I5 peer receives exactly our 2 prefixes |
| `07-tighten-max-prefix` [Lower the customer maximum-prefix from 100 to 50](corpus/07-tighten-max-prefix.md) | hygiene | safe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | nothing |
| `08-upstream-timers` [Shorten BGP timers toward the upstream](corpus/08-upstream-timers.md) | hygiene | safe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | nothing |
| `09-customer-localpref` [Lower customer local-preference from 300 to 250](corpus/09-customer-localpref.md) | traffic-engineering | safe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | nothing |
| `10-transit-export-filter-removed` [Upstream export filter replaced with permit-all](corpus/10-transit-export-filter-removed.md) | route-leak | unsafe | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | ✅ | I4 no peer route leaked to upstream; I5 upstream receives exactly our 2 prefixes |
| `11-peer-export-filter-removed` [Peer export filter replaced with permit-all](corpus/11-peer-export-filter-removed.md) | route-leak | unsafe | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | ✅ | I4 no upstream route leaked to peer; I4 no default leaked to peer; I5 peer receives exactly our 2 prefixes |
| `12-ibgp-send-community-dropped` [send-community removed on the pe1 to pe2 iBGP session](corpus/12-ibgp-send-community-dropped.md) | policy-bug | unsafe | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | nothing |
| `13-upstream-asn-typo` [Typo in the upstream's ASN (65020 instead of 65200)](corpus/13-upstream-asn-typo.md) | fat-finger | unsafe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | I1 pe1-up1 session up; I2 upstream has customer route; I2 upstream has our aggregate; I3 customer has upstream route; I3 customer has default; I3 customer reaches upstream; I5 upstream receives exactly our 2 prefixes |
| `14-peer-session-shutdown` [Peer session administratively shut down](corpus/14-peer-session-shutdown.md) | fat-finger | unsafe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | I1 pe2-peer1 session up; I2 peer has customer route; I2 peer has our aggregate; I3 customer has peer route; I3 customer reaches peer; I5 peer receives exactly our 2 prefixes |
| `15-customer-filter-too-strict` [Customer prefix-list typo rejects the customer's /24](corpus/15-customer-filter-too-strict.md) | policy-bug | unsafe | ✅ | ❌ approved a bad change | ✅ | I2 upstream has customer route; I2 peer has customer route; I3 customer reaches upstream; I3 customer reaches peer; I5 upstream receives exactly our 2 prefixes; I5 peer receives exactly our 2 prefixes |
| `16-mass-withdrawal` [Upstream export policy denies everything](corpus/16-mass-withdrawal.md) | withdrawal | unsafe | ✅ | ❌ approved a bad change | ✅ | I2 upstream has customer route; I2 upstream has our aggregate; I3 customer reaches upstream; I5 upstream receives exactly our 2 prefixes |
| `17-default-leaked-to-peer` [default-originate configured toward the peer](corpus/17-default-leaked-to-peer.md) | route-leak | unsafe | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | ✅ | I4 no default leaked to peer; I5 peer receives exactly our 2 prefixes |
| `18-redistribute-connected` [redistribute connected added on pe1](corpus/18-redistribute-connected.md) | hygiene | unsafe | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | nothing |
| `19-nexthop-self-removed` [next-hop-self removed on pe2 toward pe1](corpus/19-nexthop-self-removed.md) | policy-bug | unsafe | ✅ | ❌ approved a bad change | ✅ | I3 customer reaches peer |
| `20-ibgp-shutdown` [iBGP session between pe1 and pe2 shut down](corpus/20-ibgp-shutdown.md) | fat-finger | unsafe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | I1 pe1-pe2 iBGP up; I2 peer has customer route; I2 peer has our aggregate; I3 customer has peer route; I3 customer reaches peer; I5 peer receives exactly our 2 prefixes |
| `21-customer-max-prefix-removed` [Customer maximum-prefix safety limit removed](corpus/21-customer-max-prefix-removed.md) | latent-risk | unsafe | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | nothing |
| `22-customer-leaks-third-party` [Customer announces someone else's prefix; our filter blocks it](corpus/22-customer-leaks-third-party.md) | filter-works | safe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | nothing |
| `23-fat-finger-third-party-origin` [pe1 accidentally originates 8.8.8.0/24](corpus/23-fat-finger-third-party-origin.md) | hijack | unsafe | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | nothing |
| `24-customer-blackholed` [Static discard route for the customer prefix on pe1](corpus/24-customer-blackholed.md) | fat-finger | unsafe | ✅ | ❌ approved a bad change | ✅ | I3 customer reaches upstream; I3 customer reaches peer |
