| `26-route-map-order-bug` [A permit-everything clause inserted before the peer export filter](corpus/26-route-map-order-bug.md) | route-leak | unsafe | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | ✅ | I4 no upstream route leaked to peer; I4 no default leaked to peer; I5 peer receives exactly our 2 prefixes |
| `27-local-asn-typo` [pe2 configured with the wrong local ASN](corpus/27-local-asn-typo.md) | fat-finger | unsafe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | I1 pe1-pe2 iBGP up; I1 pe2-peer1 session up; I2 peer has customer route; I2 peer has our aggregate; I3 customer has peer route; I3 customer reaches peer; I5 peer receives exactly our 2 prefixes |
| `28-customer-import-policy-removed` [Customer inbound route-map removed](corpus/28-customer-import-policy-removed.md) | policy-bug | unsafe | ✅ | ❌ approved a bad change | ✅ | I2 upstream has customer route; I2 peer has customer route; I3 customer reaches upstream; I3 customer reaches peer; I5 upstream receives exactly our 2 prefixes; I5 peer receives exactly our 2 prefixes |
| `29-graceful-restart` [Enable BGP graceful restart on pe1](corpus/29-graceful-restart.md) | hygiene | safe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | nothing |
| `30-peer-import-filter-removed` [Peer inbound filter replaced with permit-all](corpus/30-peer-import-filter-removed.md) | latent-risk | unsafe | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | nothing |

## Netdryrun's losses

- **`06-customer-adds-prefix` Customer announces a second allowed /24** (false block). Normal customer growth inside the registered range.
- **`12-ibgp-send-community-dropped` send-community removed on the pe1 to pe2 iBGP session** (false pass). A common mistake when rebuilding iBGP sessions.
- **`18-redistribute-connected` redistribute connected added on pe1** (false pass). Not covered by the intent spec, which has no check for infrastructure routes at the customer.
- **`21-customer-max-prefix-removed` Customer maximum-prefix safety limit removed** (false pass). Latent risk: no steady-state check can see it until the customer actually leaks. Catching it needs a failure-injection scenario (the customer sends many prefixes), planned for a later release.
- **`23-fat-finger-third-party-origin` pe1 accidentally originates 8.8.8.0/24** (false pass). Not covered by the intent spec, which has no check for unexpected routes at the customer.
- **`30-peer-import-filter-removed` Peer inbound filter replaced with permit-all** (false pass). Latent risk: invisible in steady state until the peer misbehaves. Needs a failure-injection scenario.

## Findings after the run

These findings came after the run. The table above is left exactly as pre-registered; nothing in [`corpus/cases/`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/corpus/cases) was edited.

**Case 12 was labeled wrong.** The case expected that removing `neighbor 10.0.3.2 send-community` on pe1 stops pe2 from seeing the customer community. In FRR (verified on 10.4.1) communities are sent to every neighbor by default, so deleting the explicit line is a no-op: `show running-config` no longer shows it, but pe1 still advertises `10.100.0.0/24` to pe2 with community `65000:100`, and pe2 still matches it (`show bgp ipv4 unicast community 65000:100` lists the route). Reproduce with `scripts/corpus_case12_verify.sh`. The change is actually safe, so all three strategies answered case 12 correctly. With that one label corrected the scores would be: ping only 21/30, sessions up 16/30, Netdryrun 25/30. The headline numbers stay at the pre-registered values. The mistake would have been real on platforms that do not send communities by default (Cisco IOS, for example); a vendor-specific version of this case belongs in a future corpus.

**Cases 18, 23, 21 and 30 are real misses.** 18 and 23 are gaps in the intent spec (no check for unexpected routes reaching the customer or the upstream). 21 and 30 are latent risks that no steady-state check can see; they need a failure-injection scenario where the customer or peer actually misbehaves. These stay as losses.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/how-its-built/

# How Netdryrun is built and checked

## Who writes the code

AI agents do most of the development: code, tests, docs and this website. One person directs the work, decides what ships and pushes the commits. The project is new, its first commit is from October 2026, and it has no outside contributors yet. The [commit history](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commits/main) is the record of every change.

Because of that, claims about Netdryrun should be checked against something other than the code's author. The rest of this page lists what there is to check.

## Every result can be rerun

- **The corpus is public and reruns with one command.** The [Verdict Corpus](corpus.md) is a set of BGP changes, each with [its own page](corpus.md#every-case), plus the runner ([`corpus/run.py`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/run.py)) and the raw output ([`results.json`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/results/results.json)).
- **It also reruns on GitHub's machines.** The [Reproduce corpus](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/reproduce-corpus.yml) workflow runs every case on a GitHub-hosted runner from your own fork and lists every verdict that differs from the committed results.

## The corpus verdicts were written before the runs

- **The expected verdicts were committed first.** All 30 cases, with their expected verdicts, were added in one commit, [`b4df0b0`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/b4df0b0). The results came later, in [`7576298`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/7576298). The [history of `corpus/cases/`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commits/main/corpus/cases) has no other commit: no verdict was changed after a run.
- **Limit of this evidence:** git commit dates are set by the author's machine. The history shows the order of the commits and that the cases were not edited. It is not an independent timestamp.

## Losses are published


- **Netdryrun is wrong on 6 of 30 cases**: it approved 5 harmful changes and blocked 1 safe one ([RESULTS.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/RESULTS.md)). They are shown in the same table as the catches.
    - Approved although harmful: [`12` send-community removed on the pe1 to pe2 iBGP session](corpus/12-ibgp-send-community-dropped.md), [`18` redistribute connected added on pe1](corpus/18-redistribute-connected.md), [`21` Customer maximum-prefix safety limit removed](corpus/21-customer-max-prefix-removed.md), [`23` pe1 accidentally originates 8.8.8.0/24](corpus/23-fat-finger-third-party-origin.md) and [`30` Peer inbound filter replaced with permit-all](corpus/30-peer-import-filter-removed.md).
    - Blocked although safe: [`06` Customer announces a second allowed /24](corpus/06-customer-adds-prefix.md).

- **One of our own labels was wrong.** [Case 12](corpus/12-ibgp-send-community-dropped.md) expected a change to be harmful; on FRR it is a no-op. The label stays as committed and the scores were not corrected upward; the finding and a script that reproduces it are in [AMENDMENTS.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/AMENDMENTS.md).
- **The misses are explained**, not removed: two are gaps in the intent spec ([18](corpus/18-redistribute-connected.md), [23](corpus/23-fat-finger-third-party-origin.md)) and two are risks no steady-state check can see ([21](corpus/21-customer-max-prefix-removed.md), [30](corpus/30-peer-import-filter-removed.md); [AMENDMENTS.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/AMENDMENTS.md)).

## Live labs run in CI

Every push to `main` and every pull request runs [`ci.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml) ([runs](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/actions/workflows/ci.yml)). Besides unit tests on Python 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13, three jobs boot real containerlab labs:

- **`e2e`** runs the GitHub Action against [`examples/frr-bgp`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/frr-bgp) and [`examples/srl-frr`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/srl-frr) (FRR and Nokia SR Linux). Both must pass.
- **`catches-bad-change`** runs [`examples/frr-bgp-broken`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/frr-bgp-broken), a change that leaks a default route. This job passes only if Netdryrun reports `failed` with at least one failed check.
- **`agent-demo`** replays [`examples/agent-demo`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/agent-demo): a change that leaks routes must fail on exactly the leak guards, and the proper fix must pass ([`demo.sh`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/examples/agent-demo/demo.sh)).

The SONiC and Arista EOS drivers are not in CI yet (cEOS is an image each user downloads from Arista). Their unit tests parse output captured from real lab runs ([`tests/fixtures`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/tests/fixtures)).

## Other models review the work

Before releases, the code is reviewed by AI models from other vendors (OpenAI GPT and xAI Grok) and by separate agent sessions that start without the author's context. The review transcripts are not published. The fixes they led to are: [`ec23379`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/ec23379) (v0.2.0 review fixes) and [`6495759`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/6495759) (agent demo review fixes).

These reviewers are AI models, not network engineers. No independent human audit of the code has been done.

## Bugs our own testing found

Each of these was found by running Netdryrun against live labs or the corpus. The first two are in the [0.2.0 changelog](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md#020-2026-10-27).

- **False passes on SR Linux and Arista.** A leaked route that was received but not installed was invisible, so a `present: false` check passed when it should have failed. Found by live leak tests; fixed in [`77f43d6`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/77f43d6); regression tests use captured output ([`test_drivers.py`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/tests/test_drivers.py)).
- **Wrong status after a failure scenario.** A change that broke a baseline check ended a scenario run as `error` instead of `failed`. Found by running a check pack against the corpus ([`scripts/pack_verify.sh`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/scripts/pack_verify.sh)); fixed in [`f6ea560`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/f6ea560). There is no unit test for this fix yet.
- **A mislabeled corpus case.** [Case 12](corpus/12-ibgp-send-community-dropped.md), above ([AMENDMENTS.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/AMENDMENTS.md)).

## Supply-chain checks

- **Releases** go to PyPI through Trusted Publishing, with no stored tokens ([`release.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/release.yml)).
- **OpenSSF Scorecard** scores the repository's practices every week and on every push to `main` ([`scorecard.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/scorecard.yml), [current score](https://scorecard.dev/viewer/?uri=github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun)). The score includes the checks this project does poorly on.
- **CodeQL** scans the Python code and the workflows ([`codeql.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/codeql.yml)).
- **Every third-party GitHub Action is pinned to a commit**, in the workflows and in [`action.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/action.yml).

## What we do not claim

- **Not production safety.** A pass means the change behaved correctly in a small lab running open-source or lab images of network operating systems. It does not prove the change is safe on your network ([what a lab cannot prove](trust.md#what-a-lab-cannot-prove)).
- **Not scale.** The labs have a handful of nodes and small routing tables. Nothing here is tested at full Internet table size or with hundreds of peers.
- **Not vendor parity.** FRR, SR Linux, SONiC and cEOS behave differently from each other and from hardware routers. The corpus runs only on FRR, one topology and one intent spec, all written by the Netdryrun maintainers.
- **Not adoption.** Nothing on this site claims who uses Netdryrun.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/when-to-use-what/

# When to use what

Several good open-source tools help you test network changes. They answer different questions and work well together. This page tries to describe each one fairly; if something here is wrong or out of date, please [open an issue](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues).

## The short version

| Tool | Best at | Runs routers? |
|---|---|---|
| [Batfish](https://batfish.org) | Analyzing configs of many vendors without booting anything: reachability, ACLs and firewall rules, routing, differences between two snapshots | No, it models them |
| [netlab](https://netlab.tools) | Building a working lab from a short, high-level topology, with generated configs for many platforms and built-in validation tests | Yes, through containerlab or libvirt |
| [pyATS / Genie](https://developer.cisco.com/pyats/) | A full Python test framework with a large library of device parsers, for testing labs and real (including production) devices, with state snapshots and diffs | Works against any reachable device |
| [containerlab](https://containerlab.dev) | Running container-based network labs from a YAML topology, for many network operating systems | Yes, it is the lab |
| Netdryrun™ | Declarative, convergence-aware checks on a containerlab lab, packaged for CI with a pass/fail verdict and evidence | Yes, through containerlab |

## Batfish

Batfish parses device configs and builds a model of the network's control and data plane. Because nothing has to boot, it is fast, covers large networks, and supports configs from many vendors. It can answer broad questions ("can any host in this subnet reach that server?", "what changed between these two snapshots?") that are hard to test by sending packets.

Use it when you want broad, fast analysis on every commit, especially for ACLs, firewall policy and multi-vendor configs that you cannot run in containers.

A model is not the running software, so behavior that depends on the real implementation (timers, convergence order, bugs) is outside what it sees. That is where a lab helps.

## netlab

netlab takes a compact topology description ("these routers, running OSPF and BGP, connected like this") and builds the whole lab: addressing, device configs for many platforms, and the containerlab or libvirt topology. It also includes validation tests you can run against the lab.

Use it when building and maintaining the lab is the hard part, or when you want the same design on several platforms.

It combines with Netdryrun naturally: netlab can generate a containerlab topology, and Netdryrun can run its checks against that topology as a CI gate.

## pyATS / Genie

pyATS is a mature Python test framework from Cisco, and Genie adds a large library of parsers and models that turn CLI output into structured data. It can learn the state of a device, take before and after snapshots, and diff them. It works against lab devices and real ones.

Use it when you need deep, programmable testing, broad parser coverage (especially for Cisco platforms), or pre- and post-change checks on production devices.

Netdryrun is much smaller: a YAML file and a GitHub Action, with no test code to write, and it only runs against labs. If you already have pyATS tests, keep them.

## containerlab

containerlab runs network labs from a YAML topology: container-native network operating systems (such as Nokia SR Linux, Arista cEOS, Juniper cRPD, FRR) and, through vrnetlab, many VM-based ones. It handles wiring, management addresses and lifecycle.

Use it whenever you want a real lab on a laptop or a CI runner. Netdryrun does not replace it; Netdryrun drives it.

## Netdryrun

Netdryrun adds a test layer on top of a containerlab lab:

- positive checks wait for convergence and must pass twice in a row
- negative checks (absent routes, failing pings, prefix upper bounds) run only after convergence and must hold
- a route that was received but not selected counts as present
- every run produces one pass/fail result, a CI-friendly exit code, and a JSON evidence file


It is early (version 0.3.0). Drivers exist for FRR, Nokia SR Linux, SONiC and Arista EOS (bring your own cEOS image), and checks cover BGP sessions, prefix counts, routes, BGP best-path attributes and ping, with link-down and node-isolation failure scenarios.

It does not do static analysis, build labs for you, or test production devices.

## How they combine

A reasonable pipeline uses more than one:

1. **Batfish** on every commit for fast, broad config analysis.
2. **netlab** or a hand-written **containerlab** topology to build a lab that mirrors the change.
3. **Netdryrun** in CI to boot that lab, wait for convergence, and gate the merge on runtime behavior.
4. **pyATS / Genie** (or similar) for pre- and post-change checks on the production devices during the change window.

None of these steps proves the change is safe on its own. Each one removes a different class of mistakes.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/trust/

# Trust and security

## License

Netdryrun™ is open source under the [Apache License 2.0](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/LICENSE). The source is at [github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun).

## How releases are published

- Releases are built and published by a GitHub Actions workflow when a version tag (`v*`) is pushed. The workflow checks that the tag matches the package version before building.
- Packages are uploaded to [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/netdryrun/) with **Trusted Publishing** (OpenID Connect). No PyPI token or password is stored in the repository or its secrets; PyPI accepts the upload because it comes from that workflow in that repository.
- The same workflow creates a GitHub release with the built files attached.
- The GitHub Action (`netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.0`) installs Netdryrun from the action's own source at the tag you reference. Pin a tag or a commit SHA.

## Reporting a security issue

Email **[security@netdryrun.com](mailto:security@netdryrun.com)**. Please do not open a public issue for a vulnerability. Include the version, what you found, and how to reproduce it.

## What a lab cannot prove

A Netdryrun pass means the change behaved correctly in a lab. The lab runs real routing software, so a pass is strong evidence for protocol logic and policy intent: sessions come up, the intended prefixes are accepted, routes land in the routing table, traffic gets through, and unwanted routes stay out. It does not prove:

- **Vendor-specific behavior.** Open-source and container routers (FRR, SR Linux, SONiC VS) are not your vendor's routers, and even Arista cEOS is not the same as EOS on hardware. Defaults, policy evaluation and bugs differ between implementations and versions. For Arista you can bring your own licensed cEOS image.
- **Scale.** A lab has a handful of nodes and small tables, not full Internet tables or hundreds of peers.
- **Hardware and ASIC behavior.** Containers have no forwarding hardware, so TCAM limits, hardware programming and line-rate effects are not tested.
- **Timing at scale.** Convergence time in a small lab says little about convergence time in a large production network.


Version 0.3.0 also covers only BGP (IPv4/IPv6 unicast), routes, BGP best-path attributes and ping, plus link-down and node-isolation failure scenarios. OSPF/IS-IS adjacencies and path checks are not covered yet.


## Running untrusted labs

containerlab runs privileged containers, so a topology and its configs are code that runs with root on the host. Only run labs you trust. In CI, see the [GitHub Action security notes](github-action.md#security-notes). For AI agents, see the [MCP safety model](ai-agents.md#safety-model).

## Privacy

**The tool has no telemetry.** The CLI, the GitHub Action and the MCP server do not phone home or send usage data anywhere. Reports are written only to the files you ask for (and to the GitHub Actions step summary when running in Actions). containerlab and Docker may pull images from registries named in your topology, as they normally would.

The one exception is opt-in: if you set `cloud: true` on the GitHub Action, the Action uploads the JSON report to Netdryrun Cloud. The report contains raw command output from your lab devices (configs and routing tables), which can reveal your test network's addressing and topology. Leave `cloud` off and nothing is uploaded.

**This website** is static documentation hosted on GitHub Pages. It sets no cookies, has no analytics and no forms, and serves its fonts itself, so your browser contacts no third party. GitHub, as the host, receives your IP address and request details to serve the pages.

## Trademarks

"Netdryrun" and the Netdryrun logos are trademarks of the Netdryrun project. The Apache-2.0 license covers the code, not the name: forks are welcome under a different name. See the [trademark policy](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/TRADEMARKS.md).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/support/

# Support and versioning policy

## Support

Netdryrun is free open-source software under Apache-2.0, provided as is. Support for free use is best effort through [GitHub issues](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues). Security reports get priority (see [Contact](contact.md)). There is no uptime or response-time guarantee for free use.

Only the latest release gets fixes. Upgrading is the fix for bugs in older releases.

## Version numbers

Netdryrun uses [semantic versioning](https://semver.org). Before 1.0, a minor release (0.2 to 0.3) may contain breaking changes; patch releases (0.2.0 to 0.2.1) never do. Every change is in the [changelog](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

## What counts as a breaking change

These are the interfaces other tools and agents rely on:

| Interface | Stable contract |
|---|---|
| CLI | command names, flags, and exit codes (`0` passed, `1` failed, `2` error, `3` inconclusive) |
| `netdryrun.yml` | check types and keys; a file that validated keeps validating |
| JSON report | the `schema` field (`netdryrun.report/v1`); fields are only added within a schema version, never removed or renamed |
| GitHub Action | input and output names and their meaning; pin a tag or a commit SHA |
| MCP server | tool names, their arguments, and the `status` and `verdict` fields |

Removing or renaming any of these, or changing their meaning, is a breaking change. Adding is not: a new check type, a new report field, or a new `status` value (`inconclusive` was added after 0.2.0). Treat any status you don't know as not passed.

## Deprecation

Before something is removed, it keeps working for at least one minor release with a warning that names the replacement, and the changelog says so. After 1.0, removals wait for the next major version.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/design-partners/

# Design partners

Netdryrun is young. We'd rather learn from a few real changes than guess. If you have a routing change coming up, we'll help you test it in a lab, for free, in exchange for honest feedback.

## What you get

- A runnable containerlab lab of the relevant part of your network, built with you from your sanitized configs.
- A `netdryrun.yml` with checks for what your change must do and what must never happen (leaks, lost reachability).
- The verdict with evidence, before your change goes anywhere real. You keep everything.
- Help wiring it into your CI, if you want it there.

## What we ask

- One real upcoming change, and sanitized configs for the routers involved: replace public addresses and AS numbers with documentation ranges and remove secrets. We'll help you check.
- Honest feedback: what was useful, what got in the way, how you test changes today.
- Optional: permission to publish an anonymized write-up. Nothing is published without your written OK.

## Fair warning

- A lab is not production. A pass covers the checks in the lab, on the network OSes we support ([FRR, Nokia SR Linux, SONiC, Arista EOS](reference/config.md#drivers)). See [what a lab cannot prove](trust.md#what-a-lab-cannot-prove).
- We never touch your production network and never need access to it.
- This is a small independent project, so we take a few partners at a time.

## How your configs are handled

You send sanitized configs only. They're used for your lab and nothing else, kept private, and deleted within 30 days after delivery unless you ask us to keep them. An NDA is available on request. See the [privacy notice](privacy.md).

## Apply

Run `netdryrun feedback` and tick "Design partner", or email [hello@netdryrun.com](mailto:hello@netdryrun.com) with one line about the change you want to test.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/contact/

# Contact

| What | Where | Expect an answer |
|---|---|---|
| Feedback after trying it (2 minutes) | run `netdryrun feedback`, or the [feedback form](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues/new?template=feedback.yml) | read by a human |
| Free help testing one real change | [design partners](design-partners.md) | within a few days |
| Bugs, questions, feature requests | [GitHub issues](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues) | best effort, usually within a few days |
| Security vulnerabilities (please don't open a public issue) | [security@netdryrun.com](mailto:security@netdryrun.com) or [GitHub private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/security/advisories/new) | acknowledgment within 3 days |
| Everything else: trademark permission, paid work, press | [hello@netdryrun.com](mailto:hello@netdryrun.com) | best effort, usually within a few days |

Netdryrun is a small, independent open-source project. There is no phone line and no sales team. Free use comes with best-effort support; see the [support and versioning policy](support.md).

Security researchers: our [security.txt](https://netdryrun.com/.well-known/security.txt) follows RFC 9116, and the [security policy](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/SECURITY.md) explains how reports are handled.

Source: https://netdryrun.com/privacy/

# Privacy notice

*Last updated: 27 October 2026*

## Who is responsible

Victor Khen ("we"). Netdryrun is run by an individual; no company has been formed. Contact for anything about your data: [hello@netdryrun.com](mailto:hello@netdryrun.com).

## The short version

- **The Netdryrun tool** (CLI, GitHub Action, MCP server) has no telemetry. It sends us nothing. The GitHub Action uploads a report to Netdryrun Cloud only if you set `cloud: true`; Netdryrun Cloud is not open to the public yet, and its own privacy terms will be published here before it is.
- **This website** sets no cookies, has no analytics and no forms, and serves its fonts itself.
- **We see your data only if you email us or interact with the project on GitHub.**

## This website

netdryrun.com is static documentation hosted on GitHub Pages. To deliver the pages, GitHub processes your IP address and request details (page, time, browser) under the [GitHub privacy statement](https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/privacy-policies/github-general-privacy-statement). We do not receive these logs. If you switch between light and dark mode, your browser remembers the choice in its local storage; that stays on your device. Search runs entirely in your browser.

## Email

When you write to an @netdryrun.com address, Cloudflare Email Routing forwards the message to our mailbox. We use your address and message only to answer you and keep the conversation for as long as it's useful, then delete it. Security reports may be kept as records of how the issue was handled. Lawful basis: our legitimate interest in answering you.

## GitHub and PyPI

Issues, pull requests and discussions on [github.com/netdryrun](https://github.com/netdryrun) are public and governed by GitHub's terms and privacy statement. Downloads from PyPI are handled by the Python Software Foundation under the [PyPI privacy notice](https://policies.python.org/pypi.org/Privacy-Notice/). We don't combine this information with anything else.

## Transfers

GitHub and Cloudflare are based in the United States. Transfers of personal data from the EU or UK rely on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (and its UK extension) where the company is certified, and on the European Commission's standard contractual clauses otherwise.

## Your rights

You can ask for access to, correction of, or deletion of your personal data, a copy of it, restriction of processing, or object to processing based on legitimate interest. Email [hello@netdryrun.com](mailto:hello@netdryrun.com); we answer within 30 days. You can also complain to your data protection authority.

## Changes

We update this notice when what we do with data changes, for example before Netdryrun Cloud or paid products launch, and change the date at the top.
